title: Preface
summary:
- Best Buy Co., Inc.’s Annual Report on Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended February 2, 2019 (Commission File No. 1-9595), filed as a large accelerated filer and NYSE-listed company.
- Company identification details: Minnesota incorporation, EIN 41-0907483, headquarters at 7601 Penn Avenue South, Richfield, MN 55423; common stock par value $0.10.
- Compliance and status disclosures: timely SEC filings, Interactive Data File submission, not a shell company; market value of non-affiliate equity as of August 3, 2018, and shares outstanding as of March 26, 2019.
- Documents incorporated by reference: portions of the 2019 Proxy Statement.
- Cautionary forward-looking statements under the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act, referencing Item 1A Risk Factors.
- Table of contents outlining Parts I–IV, including Business, Risk Factors, Properties, Legal Proceedings, MD&A, Market Risk, Financial Statements, Controls and Procedures, and governance/compensation items.
- Item 1 Business overview: mission to enrich consumers’ lives through technology across online, in-store, and in-home channels; operations in the U.S., Canada, and Mexico.
- Segment structure: two reportable segments—Domestic (Best Buy, bestbuy.com, Best Buy Mobile, Geek Squad, GreatCall, Magnolia, Pacific Kitchen and Home) and International (Canada and Mexico, including bestbuy.ca and bestbuy.com.mx).
- Strategic actions: closure of all 257 U.S. Best Buy Mobile stand-alone stores during fiscal 2019; acquisition of GreatCall, Inc. on October 1, 2018, expanding into connected health services for aging consumers.
- Operating model: centralized merchandising, pricing, marketing, supply chain, and support functions; standardized store procedures; field operations supporting retail, services, and in-home teams; International operations similar to Domestic.
- Merchandise and services framework organized into six revenue categories: Computing and Mobile Phones, Consumer Electronics, Appliances, Entertainment, Services, and Other, addressing customer needs in entertainment, productivity, communication, food preparation, security, and health and wellness.

- Context and scope: Excerpt from Item 1. Business in Best Buy Co., Inc.’s Form 10-K (Part I), with a note that “we/us/our” refers to Best Buy Co., Inc. and consolidated subsidiaries, and website references are not incorporated by reference.
- Company overview: Incorporated in Minnesota in 1966; mission to enrich consumers’ lives through technology across entertainment, productivity, communication, food preparation, security, and health/wellness; operations in the U.S., Canada, and Mexico.
- Segments and brands: Two reportable segments—Domestic and International. Domestic covers all U.S. operations under brands including Best Buy, bestbuy.com, Best Buy Direct, Best Buy Express, Best Buy Mobile, Geek Squad, GreatCall, Magnolia, and Pacific Kitchen and Home. International includes Canada and Mexico under Best Buy, Best Buy Express, Best Buy Mobile, Geek Squad, bestbuy.ca, and bestbuy.com.mx.
- Strategic actions: Closure of all 257 remaining U.S. Best Buy Mobile stand-alone stores (announced March 1, 2018; completed in Q2 FY2019). Acquisition of GreatCall, Inc. on October 1, 2018, a connected health services provider for aging consumers. Cross-references to MD&A and Notes for details.
- Operating model: Both segments use a multi-channel platform (online, in-store, in-home). Centralized management of merchandising, services, pricing, promotions, procurement/supply chain, digital operations, marketing, labor, and corporate support (HR, finance, real estate). Standardized store procedures with local flexibility; field operations support retail, services, and in-home teams. International operations are similar to Domestic.
- Governance: Each segment has leadership teams responsible for all business areas.
- Merchandise and services: Six revenue categories—Computing & Mobile Phones, Consumer Electronics, Appliances, Entertainment, Services, and Other—targeting key consumer needs across the areas noted above.
- References: Points to Item 7 (MD&A) and Item 8 (Financial Statements and Supplementary Data), including Note 2 (Acquisition) and Note 9 (Restructuring Charges), for further details.

summary:
- Document type and scope: Part I of Best Buy Co., Inc.’s Form 10-K, covering Item 1 (Business) and the start of Item 1A (Risk Factors).
- Company overview: Incorporated in Minnesota in 1966; purpose is to enrich lives through technology across online, in-store, and in-home channels in the U.S., Canada, and Mexico.
- Segments and brands: Two reportable segments—Domestic (U.S.) and International (Canada and Mexico)—operating under brands such as Best Buy, bestbuy.com, Best Buy Mobile, Geek Squad, Magnolia, Pacific Kitchen and Home, GreatCall, and others.
- Strategic changes: Closed all 257 U.S. standalone Best Buy Mobile stores in fiscal 2019; acquired GreatCall, Inc. on October 1, 2018 to expand connected health services for aging consumers.
- Operating model: Centrally managed merchandising, pricing, promotions, supply chain, digital operations, marketing, and support functions; standardized store procedures with local flexibility; International operations broadly mirror Domestic.
- Revenue categories: Six categories—Computing and Mobile Phones; Consumer Electronics; Appliances; Entertainment; Services (including memberships, protection plans, in-home, and GreatCall); and Other (including sundries and select categories in International).
- Omnichannel distribution: Options for ship-from-store, ship-from-DC, and buy online, pick up in store; similar models in Canada and Mexico; direct-to-store shipments for certain product releases.
- Supplier concentration and inventory: Top 20 suppliers comprise ~64% of merchandise spend; Apple, Samsung, HP, Sony, and LG represent ~51%; typically no long-term supply contracts; active inventory management with vendor funding for markdowns/returns; global sourcing for exclusive brands.
- Store footprint and strategy: 1,187 large-format and 51 small-format stores at fiscal 2019 year-end; stores integral to omnichannel advantage; all U.S. stores and Canada large-format enabled for ship-from-store; store-within-a-store vendor concepts; ongoing space optimization, lease renegotiations, selective openings/closures.
- Intellectual property: Portfolio of trademarks and patents (e.g., Best Buy, Geek Squad, Insignia, Magnolia, GreatCall, Jitterbug, Lively, Yellow Tag logo); IP viewed as a key marketing and brand asset.
- Seasonality and working capital: Heavily weighted to fiscal Q4 (holiday season); funded by cash, investments, operating cash flow, and revolving credit; working capital needs rise pre-holiday.
- Competitive landscape: Competition from multi-channel and online retailers, technology service providers, traditional retailers, vendors, and carriers; heightened price transparency; Wayfair decision eroding online-only sales tax advantage; Best Buy emphasizes price competitiveness, price matching, scale efficiencies, vendor partnerships, services, and integrated assets.
- Environmental and social initiatives: Expanded employee benefits (mental health, backup childcare, caregiver leave, PTO for part-time); D&I commitments (CEO Action, Parity Pledge); Best Buy Teen Tech Centers (25 active, goal of 60); progress toward 60% carbon reduction by 2020; promote ENERGY STAR products; recycled 180+ million pounds of electronics/appliances in fiscal 2019.
- Workforce: Nearly 125,000 employees across the U.S., Canada, and Mexico; competitive, locally appropriate benefits.
- Public disclosures and governance: SEC filings and governance documents available on the investor website; includes charters for Board committees and codes of ethics.
- Risk factors (partial): Emphasizes intense competition, growing price transparency, online and mobile sales trends, and rising delivery expectations that can pressure revenue and profitability; notes that listed risks could materially affect results and are not exhaustive.

ey terms of our arrangements.We carefully monito

title: Risk Factors.
heading: Item 1A. Risk Factors.
start_phrase: Described below are certain risks that we believe apply to our business and the industry in which we operate.
summary:
- Overview and disclosures: Notes to corporate responsibility and sustainability efforts, including helping customers save on utility bills and recycling 180+ million pounds of electronics/appliances in fiscal 2019. Workforce size of ~125,000 across the U.S., Canada and Mexico with competitive, locally tailored benefits. Availability of SEC filings, governance documents, and codes of ethics on Best Buy’s investor website; documents also obtainable via written request.
- Item 1A. Risk Factors (summary of key risks):
  - Competitive landscape: Intense competition from omnichannel retailers, e-commerce, vendors, technology service providers, and mobile carriers; heightened price transparency; delivery speed/cost pressures; higher cost structure tied to service-centric strategy can compress margins.
  - Expansion into new products/services/technologies: Limited experience and scaling risk in new segments; potential technology failures and service disruptions; added regulatory exposure (e.g., HIPAA) and liability, particularly with healthcare-related services and the GreatCall acquisition.
  - Services strategy risks: Higher labor costs; fulfillment errors/omissions; uncertain warranty failure rates; in-home and managed services liability; device/data handling risks; third-party installer compliance; evolving service-related regulations.
  - Vendor and carrier dependence: Concentration among top suppliers; limited long-term contracts; vulnerability to unfavorable terms, assortment/allocation decisions, or vendor disintermediation; dependence on a few mobile carriers and their shifting policies.
  - Talent and labor: Challenges attracting, retaining, and engaging qualified employees; sector-high turnover; wage inflation pressures; potential impact from executive/key employee turnover.
  - Regulatory/legal environment: Complex, sometimes conflicting requirements across jurisdictions; environmental, product safety/transport, data privacy/security (e.g., CCPA), financial reform, labor rules, healthcare, pricing/content/mobile/payments regulations; trade/tariff changes; tax law changes; litigation trends (including class actions).
  - Macroeconomic conditions: Sensitivity to GDP, consumer confidence, inflation, employment, interest rates, credit availability, housing, FX, fuel/food costs, and geopolitical events impacting consumer demand and upgrade cycles.
  - Cost management: Fixed and multi-year cost structures amid revenue volatility; need for ongoing efficiency; failure to control costs could limit growth and profitability.
  - IT systems and cybersecurity: Dependence on internal and vendor IT systems for core operations; risks from outages, attacks, disasters, and scalability issues; potential service disruptions to web/mobile platforms.
  - Data privacy and security: Exposure from handling customer (including payment), employee, vendor, and company data; third-party system risks; device servicing and product code vulnerabilities; rising compliance and insurance costs (GDPR/CCPA); potential fines, claims, and reputational harm.
  - Strategic ventures/M&A: Uncertainty in forecasting, integration challenges, internal control risks, failure to realize synergies, partner disputes, and potential impairments; management distraction and capital diversion.
  - Seasonality: Disproportionate reliance on fiscal Q4/holiday season; susceptibility to disruptions (competition, sourcing, systems, cyber, disasters).
  - Product cycles and consumer preferences: Rapid technological change, category cannibalization, price declines; risks of mis-forecasting, excess/insufficient inventory, delayed merchandising/supply chain adjustments, and brand damage.
  - Promotional financing/credit cards: Dependence on third-party banks; program profitability sensitive to transaction volumes, offer terms, bad debt, rates, regulation, and operating costs; potential impact on sales and profit-share income.
  - Supply chain/logistics: Reliance on vendors and third parties; risks from capacity limits, system changes, sector consolidation, labor actions, damage/loss, transportation cost increases; dependence on a few small-parcel carriers; need for optimal inventory positioning.
  - Catastrophic events: Natural disasters, extreme weather, epidemics, terrorism/civil unrest; impacts on workforce, stores, supply chain, IT systems, and fulfillment.
  - Brand and reputation: Service quality, pricing, delivery performance, and external negative publicity (amplified by social media) can affect sales, loyalty, hiring, and partnerships.
  - Product safety/quality: Compliance failures and recalls can trigger legal exposure, government action, sourcing challenges, and revenue/profit impacts.
  - Labor/employment law changes: Unionization risks; evolving rules on independent contractors, minimum wage, paid leave, scheduling; potential cost increases and operating model impacts.
  - Real estate portfolio: Long-term lease obligations; risks in store location/format/assortment decisions; potential closures, remodel costs, excess lease expenses, and sublease liabilities.
  - Liquidity and capital markets: Need for adequate liquidity via operations, cash, credit facilities, and payables; risks from tightened vendor terms, financing availability/costs, and credit ratings downgrades.
  - Third-party dependencies: Material reliance on partners for IT, cloud, HR ops, loyalty, financing/credit cards, gift cards, warranties, delivery/installation, support, transportation, and insurance; disruptions could hinder operations and raise costs.
  - Exclusive brands (Dynex, Insignia, Modal, Platinum, Rocketfish): Manufactured largely in Southeast Asia; heightened warranty/product liability, regulatory, logistics, obsolescence, labor/environmental compliance, IP/royalty, tariff/trade dispute, and conflict minerals risks; need to maintain quality, availability, and pricing.
  - Global sourcing: Political/economic instability, trade restrictions/tariffs, quality/safety issues, labor actions, port delays, FX, transport capacity/costs, inflation, unrest, disasters, pandemics; vendor investment and incentive changes.
  - International operations: Additional risks in Canada/Mexico retail and Asia manufacturing, including geopolitical, economic/FX, trade policy, cultural, labor relations, IP enforcement, and remote oversight; potential impairments/exit costs.
  - Forward-looking statements/guidance: Inherent forecasting uncertainty; fixed cost base; potential stock price declines if results miss guidance or guidance is reduced.
- Item 1B. Unresolved Staff Comments: Not applicable.

start_phrase:

summary:
- Market and dividends: Best Buy’s common stock trades on the NYSE under “BBY.” The company has paid regular quarterly cash dividends since fiscal 2004, issued special dividends in Q1 fiscal 2016 and 2017, and on February 28, 2019 increased the regular quarterly dividend from $0.45 to $0.50 per share. Future dividends depend on earnings, capital needs, financial condition, and other factors.
- Holders: As of March 26, 2019, there were 267,804,388 holders of record of the company’s common stock.
- Share repurchases: On February 23, 2019, the Board authorized a new $3.0 billion share repurchase program, superseding the February 2017 $5.0 billion authorization (with $1.5 billion remaining as of February 2, 2019). In fiscal 2019, the company repurchased and retired 21.2 million shares for $1.5 billion; from fiscal year-end to March 26, 2019, it repurchased an additional 0.9 million shares for $62 million. In Q4 fiscal 2019, 5.8 million shares were repurchased at an average price of $60.12, with $1.536 billion remaining under the 2017 program at quarter-end; a footnote notes $1.9 billion was available at the start of Q4 and $349 million was used during the quarter.
- Stock performance graph: Presents five-year cumulative total shareholder return versus the S&P 500 and S&P Retailing Group, assuming $100 invested at the end of fiscal 2014. As of February 2, 2019: Best Buy $290.98; S&P 500 $168.19; S&P Retailing Group $256.26. Includes a standard disclaimer that the graph is not soliciting material nor deemed filed.
- Selected financial data (five-year highlights):
  - Revenue: $42.9B (2019), $42.2B (2018), $39.4B (2017), $39.5B (2016), $40.3B (2015).
  - Operating income around $1.9B in 2019 and 2018.
  - Net earnings from continuing operations: $1.464B (2019), $0.999B (2018), $1.207B (2017), $0.807B (2016), $1.246B (2015).
  - EPS from continuing operations: $5.20 (2019), $3.26 (2018), $3.74 (2017), $2.30 (2016), $3.53 (2015). Cash dividends declared and paid per share: $1.80 (2019), $1.36 (2018), $1.57 (2017), $1.43 (2016), $0.72 (2015).
  - Operating stats: Comparable sales growth 4.8% (2019) and 5.6% (2018); gross profit rate 23.2% (2019); SG&A rate 18.7% (2019); operating income rate 4.4% (2019).
  - Year-end: Current ratio 1.2 (2019); total assets $12.9B; debt $1.388B; equity $3.306B. Store count declined over time: Domestic 1,026 and International 212 (total 1,238) in 2019; total retail square footage 44.1M.
  - Footnotes: Fiscal 2019 includes restructuring charges ($46M pre-tax), GreatCall acquisition-related charges and amortization ($35M pre-tax), and a one-time bonus related to U.S. tax reform ($7M pre-tax), plus $25M of subsequent Tax Act adjustments. Fiscal 2018 included 53 weeks.

summary:
This partial document is Item 6: Selected Financial Data from Best Buy Co., Inc.’s Form 10-K, presenting five-year financial highlights (FY2015–FY2019) to be read with MD&A (Item 7) and the audited financial statements (Item 8).

Key contents and highlights:
- Consolidated results (in millions): Revenue rose from $40.3B (2015) to $42.9B (2019); operating income hovered around $1.4B–$1.9B, reaching $1.9B in 2019; net earnings from continuing operations increased to $1.464B in 2019 (from $999M in 2018). Discontinued operations had minimal impact in recent years.
- Per-share data: EPS from continuing operations was $5.20 in 2019 (vs. $3.26 in 2018); total EPS matched $5.20 in 2019; cash dividends per share increased to $1.80 in 2019.
- Operating metrics: Comparable sales growth was 4.8% in 2019 (5.6% in 2018); gross profit rate at 23.2% (down from 24.0% in 2017); SG&A rate at 18.7%; operating income rate steady at 4.4% in 2019.
- Year-end financial position: Current ratio 1.2 (2019); total assets $12.9B; debt $1.39B; total equity $3.31B.
- Store footprint: Continued rationalization—domestic stores declined to 1,026 and international to 212 (total 1,238 in 2019); total retail square footage decreased to 44.1M from 48.2M in 2015.
- Notable footnotes/adjustments (2019): Includes $46M restructuring charges ($35M net of tax); $35M in GreatCall acquisition-related costs including intangible amortization ($28M net); $7M one-time employee bonus tied to U.S. Tax Cuts and Jobs Act ($5M net); and $25M of subsequent Tax Act adjustments. Fiscal 2018 included a 53rd week; all other years had 52 weeks.

- Presents Best Buy’s Item 6 Selected Financial Data with five-year financial highlights (2015–2019), including revenue, operating income, net earnings (including/discontinued operations), EPS, dividends, comparable sales growth, gross margin, SG&A rate, operating margin, current ratio, total assets, debt, equity, store counts by segment, and retail square footage.
- Notes key one-time or non-recurring items affecting results:
  - 2019: Restructuring charges; GreatCall acquisition-related costs and intangible amortization; one-time employee bonus tied to U.S. tax reform; Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) subsequent adjustments.
  - 2018 (53-week year): One-time employee bonus and Best Buy Foundation contribution tied to TCJA; significant TCJA charges.
  - 2017: Net benefit from CRT/LCD litigation settlements (net of fees).
  - 2016: Restructuring charges.
  - 2015: Discrete tax benefit from reorganizing European legal entities.
- Details methodology for comparable sales:
  - Includes stores, websites, and call centers open at least 14 months; exclusions for relocations/remodels; timing for acquisitions entering comp base.

  - Excludes FY2018’s extra week from comps.
  - Excludes revenue from U.S. Best Buy Mobile stand-alone stores beginning March 2018 (due to planned closures).
  - Excludes GreatCall from FY2019 comps per acquisition policy.
- Clarifies definitions: current ratio calculation; store counts include Outlet Centers.
- Introduces Item 7 MD&A structure: Overview, Business Strategy, Results of Operations, Liquidity and Capital Resources, Critical Accounting Estimates, New Accounting Pronouncements.
- Company overview highlights:
  - Mission to enrich consumers’ lives through technology across entertainment, productivity, communication, food prep, security, and health/wellness.
  - Operations in the U.S., Canada, and Mexico; two reportable segments (Domestic, which includes GreatCall, and International).
  - Fiscal year ends on the Saturday nearest end of January; FY2018 had 53 weeks, FY2019 and FY2017 had 52 weeks.
  - Business is highly seasonal with a substantial portion of revenue and earnings in fiscal Q4 (holiday period).

start_phrase: Management's Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations ("MD&A") is intended to provide a reader of our financial statements with a narrative from the perspective of our management on our financial condition, results of operations, liquidity and certain other factors that may affect our future results.

ancial Condition and Results of Operations ("MD&A") is intended to provide a reader of our financial statementswith a narrative from

e noted, transactions and other factors significantly impacting our financial condition, results of operations and liquidity arediscussed in order of magnitud

title: Overview
heading: Overview
start_phrase: We strive to enrich the lives of consumers through technology, whether they connect with us online, visit our stores or invite us into their homes.
summary:
- Footnotes detailing notable items affecting reported results:
  - Fiscal 2018: one-time employee bonus ($80M pre-tax), Best Buy Foundation contribution ($20M pre-tax), and $283M of charges from the U.S. Tax Cuts and Jobs Act.
  - Fiscal 2017: $161M from CRT and LCD litigation settlements (net of related legal costs).
  - Fiscal 2016: $201M in restructuring charges ($159M net of taxes).
  - Fiscal 2015: $353M discrete tax benefit from reorganizing European legal entities.
- Comparable sales methodology:
  - Includes stores, websites, and call centers operating at least 14 full months; excludes relocated/remodeled stores for 14 months, discontinued operations, foreign currency effects (International only), and the extra week in fiscal 2018.
  - Acquisitions included beginning the first full quarter after the first anniversary.
  - Canadian brand consolidation (Future Shop closures/conversions and website elimination) removed Canadian revenue from comps from Q1 FY2016 to Q3 FY2017; International comps resumed in Q4 FY2017.
  - U.S. Best Buy Mobile stand-alone store revenue excluded from comps beginning March 2018 due to planned closures.
  - GreatCall acquisition (Oct 1, 2018) excluded from fiscal 2019 comparable sales.
- Definitions/other metrics:
  - Current ratio = total current assets ÷ total current liabilities.
  - Store counts include Best Buy Outlet Centers.
- MD&A framework:
  - Purpose is to discuss financial condition, results, liquidity, and factors affecting future results.
  - Sections: Overview; Business Strategy; Results of Operations; Liquidity and Capital Resources; Critical Accounting Estimates; New Accounting Pronouncements.
- Company overview and reporting:
  - Mission to enrich lives through technology across multiple need areas; operations in the U.S., Canada, and Mexico.
  - Two reportable segments: Domestic (includes GreatCall) and International.
  - Fiscal year ends near end of January; FY2019 and FY2017 had 52 weeks; FY2018 had 53 weeks with the extra week in Q4.
  - Business is highly seasonal with a concentration in Q4 (holiday season).
- Non-GAAP financial measures:
  - Use of constant currency, non-GAAP operating income, non-GAAP effective tax rate, and non-GAAP diluted EPS.
  - Adjustments may include restructuring, goodwill impairments, gains/losses on investments, certain acquisition-related costs, and related tax effects; caution that measures are supplemental and may not be comparable across companies.
  - Explanation of constant currency methodology.
  - Policy change beginning Q1 FY2018: no longer excluding non-restructuring property and equipment impairment charges from non-GAAP results, reflecting transition from Renew Blue to Best Buy 2020.

title: Non-GAAP Financial Measures
heading: Non-GAAP Financial Measures
start_phrase: This MD&A includes financial information prepared in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States ("GAAP"), as well as certain adjusted or non-GAAP financial measures, such as constant currency, non-GAAP operating income,
summary:
- Comparable sales methodology: Defines comparable sales across stores, websites, and call centers operating at least 14 full months; excludes relocated/remodeled/expanded/downsized stores closed >14 days until 14 months post-reopen, acquisitions until first full quarter after 1-year anniversary, discontinued operations, foreign currency fluctuations (International only), and the extra week in fiscal 2018. Details unique events: Canadian brand consolidation (Future Shop closures/conversions) removed all Canadian revenue from comps from Q1 FY2016–Q3 FY2017; International comps resumed in Q4 FY2017 but not provided for FY2017 due to limited comparability. U.S. Best Buy Mobile stand-alone store closures (announced March 1, 2018) excluded from comps starting March 2018. GreatCall acquisition (Oct 1, 2018) excluded from FY2019 comps.
- Non-GAAP financial measures: Uses and rationale for non-GAAP metrics (constant currency, non-GAAP operating income, non-GAAP effective tax rate, non-GAAP diluted EPS), typical adjustments (restructuring, goodwill impairments, gains/losses on investments, acquisition-related costs, and related taxes), and caution on comparability. Explains constant currency methodology. Policy change beginning Q1 FY2018 to no longer exclude non-restructuring property and equipment impairments from non-GAAP results (a change from the Renew Blue era); prior periods recast; expectation that future such impairments will be immaterial.
- Business strategy and FY2019 performance highlights: Enterprise comparable sales up 4.8% (on top of 5.6% in FY2018); GAAP diluted EPS up 59.5% to $5.20; non-GAAP diluted EPS up 20.4% to $5.32; revenue $42.9B; GAAP operating income $1.9B; non-GAAP operating income $2.0B; $2.0B returned to shareholders via buybacks and dividends. Strategic progress under Best Buy 2020: launch of Total Tech Support; expansion of In-Home Advisors (~530 advisors, 175k free in-home consultations); acquisition of GreatCall to grow Health/aging-in-place services; supply chain transformation to enhance fulfillment and customer experience. Cost reductions/efficiencies of $265M in FY2019, $500M cumulative toward a $600M goal by end of FY2021. Recognition as Barron’s #1 Most Sustainable Company. FY2020 priorities: grow Total Tech Support membership, expand Health business and In-Home Advisors, advance omnichannel experiences (website/app/other channels), continue supply chain automation and process improvements to expand fulfillment and speed delivery/installation, and continue cost reductions.
- Results of operations context: Mexico operations consolidated on a one-month reporting lag; policy to accelerate recognition of significant lag-period events (none identified for presented periods). Discontinued operations primarily relate to Jiangsu Five Star within International; discussion otherwise refers to continuing operations. Fiscal 2019 and 2017 had 52 weeks; fiscal 2018 had 53 weeks (extra week in Q4).
text:
Non-GAAP Financial Measures
This MD&A includes financial in
formation prepared in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States ("GAAP"), as well as certainadjusted or non-GAAP financial measu
res, such as constant currency, non-GAAP operating income, non-GAAP effective tax rate and non-GAAP diluted earningsper share ("EPS") from continuing op
erations. We believe that non-GAAP financial measures, when reviewed in conjunction with GAAP financial measures, canprovide more informat
ion to assist investors in evaluating current period performance and in assessing future performance. For these reasons, our internalmanagement reporting 
also includes non-GAAP financial measures. Generally, our non-GAAP financial measures include adjustments for items such asrestructuring charges, goodwi
ll impairments, gains and losses on investments, certain acquisition-related costs and the tax effect of all such items. In addition,certain other ite
ms may be excluded from non-GAAP financial measures when we believe doing so provides greater clarity to management and our investors.These non-GAAP financial measures should b
e considered in addition to, and not superior to or as a substitute for, GAAP financial measures. We stronglyencourage investors and shar
eholders to review our financial statements and publicly-filed reports in their entirety and not to rely on any single financial measure.Non-GAAP financial measures as presen
ted herein may not be comparable to similarly titled measures used by other companies.In our discussions of the operat
ing results of our Consolidated business and our International segment, we sometimes refer to the impact of changes in foreigncurrency exchange rates or
 the impact of foreign currency exchange rate fluctuations, which are references to the differences between the foreign currencyexchange rates we use to conve
rt the International segment’s operating results from local currencies into U.S. dollars for reporting purposes. We also may use theterm "constant currency,"
 which represents results adjusted to exclude foreign currency impacts. We calculate those impacts as the difference between the currentperiod results transla
ted using the current period currency exchange rates and using the comparable prior period currency exchange rates. We believe the disclosureof revenue changes in constan
t currency provides useful supplementary information to investors in light of significant fluctuations in currency rates.Beginning in the first quart
er of fiscal 2018, we no longer exclude non-restructuring property and equipment impairment charges from our non-GAAP financialmetrics. When we began to ex
ecute our Renew Blue transformation in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2013, we adopted a change to non-GAAP reporting to excludenon-restructuring proper
ty and equipment impairment charges from our non-GAAP results. From that point, through the fourth quarter of fiscal 2017, we believedthat reporting non-GAAP results that 
excluded these charges provided a supplemental view of our ongoing performance that was useful and relevant to ourinvestors. Now that Renew Blue has ended and Best Buy 2020 has of
ficially launched, we believe it is no longer necessary to adjust for non-restructuring propertyand equipment impairm
ents in our non-GAAP reporting. We believe that future such impairments will predominantly be immaterial and incurred in the ordinaryscope of ongoing operations.

title: Business Strategy
heading: Business Strategy
start_phrase: On a full-year basis in fiscal 2019, we grew our Enterprise comparable sales by 4.8% on top of 5.6% in fiscal 2018, increased GAAP diluted EPS by 59.5% to $5.20 and increased our non-GAAP diluted EPS by 20.4% to $5.32.
summary:
- Non-GAAP reporting update: Beginning Q1 fiscal 2018, the company no longer adjusts for non-restructuring property and equipment impairments; prior-period non-GAAP figures were recast. A reconciliation of non-GAAP items affecting operating income, effective tax rate, and diluted EPS is referenced.
- Fiscal 2019 performance: Enterprise comparable sales up 4.8% (on top of 5.6% in fiscal 2018); GAAP diluted EPS up 59.5% to $5.20; non-GAAP diluted EPS up 20.4% to $5.32; revenue of $42.9B; GAAP operating income of $1.9B and non-GAAP operating income of $2.0B; $2.0B returned to shareholders via repurchases and dividends.
- Strategy execution (Best Buy 2020): Launched Total Tech Support (unlimited Geek Squad support); expanded In-Home Advisors from ~300 to ~530 with 175,000+ free in-home consultations; acquired GreatCall to advance health/aging-in-place services; advanced supply chain transformation to enhance fulfillment and customer experience.
- Cost efficiency progress: Achieved $265M in annualized reductions in fiscal 2019; $500M cumulative toward a $600M target by end of fiscal 2021.
- CSR/Sustainability: Recognized as No. 1 on Barron’s “100 Most Sustainable Companies” list.
- Fiscal 2020 priorities: Grow Total Tech Support membership; expand Health business; continue scaling In-Home Advisors; innovate integrated omnichannel experiences (website, app, stores); progress supply chain automation and process improvements to expand fulfillment, speed delivery, and enhance delivery/installation; continue cost reductions.
- Results of operations notes: Mexico operations consolidated on a one-month lag with acceleration policy for significant lag events (none identified); discontinued operations primarily relate to Five Star (China) and are presented separately; discussion focuses on continuing operations; fiscal 2018 included 53 weeks vs. 52 weeks in fiscal 2019 and 2017.

cal 2019, we grew our Enterprise comparable sales by 4.8% on top of 5.6% in fiscal 2018, increased GAAP diluted EPS by 59.5% to$5.20 and increased our non-GAAP diluted EPS by 20.4% to $5.32. In addi

illion in fiscal 2019. From a capital allocation standpoint, we returned $2.0 billion to our shareholders throughshare repurchases and divid

anding what we do for our customers and how we interact with them. The first example is the launch of our Total Tech Support program.Having a service that provid

l 2018 to reach $600 million by the end of fiscal 2021.In addition to these acco
mplishments, we are proud of our progress in advancing our Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability efforts. In fact, we werejust named number one on Barron’s

er customer relationships, and the related value creation opportunities that this entails.In fiscal 2020, our priorit

title: Fiscal 2019 Results Compared With Fiscal 2018
heading: Fiscal 2019 Results Compared With Fiscal 2018
start_phrase: Consolidated revenue of $42.9 billion in fiscal 2019 increased 1.7% compared to fiscal 2018.
summary:
- Consolidated performance summary for fiscal years 2019, 2018, and 2017, including revenue, comparable sales growth, gross profit and rate, SG&A and rate, restructuring charges, operating income and margin, net earnings (continuing and total), and diluted EPS (continuing and total).
- Headline trends:
  - Revenue: $42.9B in 2019 (+1.7%), $42.2B in 2018 (+7.0%), $39.4B in 2017.
  - Comparable sales growth: 4.8% (2019), 5.6% (2018), 0.3% (2017).
  - Gross profit rate declined over the period (23.2% in 2019 vs. 23.4% in 2018 vs. 24.0% in 2017).
  - SG&A rate improved (18.7% in 2019 vs. 19.0% in 2018 vs. 19.2% in 2017).
  - Operating margin held at 4.4% in 2019 (down from 4.7% in 2017).
  - Net earnings from continuing operations rose to $1.46B in 2019; diluted EPS from continuing operations $5.20 (vs. $3.26 in 2018).
  - Discontinued operations gains present in 2017 and 2018, none in 2019.
- Methodology and comparability notes:
  - Comparable sales adjustments due to Canadian brand consolidation (Future Shop closures/conversions and website elimination), with International comps paused through Q3 FY2017 and resumed in Q4 FY2017.
  - Comparable sales exclude the extra week in fiscal 2018, sales from U.S. Best Buy Mobile stand-alone stores beginning March 2018, and GreatCall results in fiscal 2019.
  - Non-comparable sales include impacts from the extra week (about $760M in 2018), store openings/closures, GreatCall results, and certain revenue streams (profit-share, specific credit card revenue, gift card breakage, commercial, and wholesale/dealer sales).
  - Caution on comparing gross profit and SG&A rates across retailers due to different supply chain cost classifications.
- Fiscal 2019 vs. 2018:
  - Revenue bridge: +4.4 pts from comparable sales, -2.5 pts from non-comparable sales (including the prior-year extra week and GreatCall classification), -0.2 pts from FX, net +1.7%.
  - Gross profit and SG&A rate movements primarily driven by the Domestic segment.
  - Restructuring charges increased to $46M (primarily Domestic).
  - Operating income up $57M; margin flat as lower gross profit rate was offset by lower SG&A rate.
- Fiscal 2018 vs. 2017:
  - Revenue bridge: +5.3 pts from comparable sales, +1.5 pts from non-comparable sales (including the extra week), +0.2 pts from FX, net +7.0%.
  - Gross profit rate down 60 bps (Domestic -40 bps; International -20 bps).
  - SG&A rate down 20 bps (Domestic -10 bps; International -10 bps).
  - Restructuring charges declined to $10M from $39M (primarily Domestic).
  - Operating income down $11M; margin decreased to 4.4%.
- Domestic segment detail:
  - Revenue: $39.3B in 2019 (+1.7%); comparable sales +4.8%.
  - Gross profit rate: 23.3% (vs. 23.4% in 2018); SG&A rate: 18.6% (vs. 18.9% in 2018).
  - Restructuring charges: $47M (vs. $9M in 2018).
  - Operating income: $1.80B; margin 4.6% (vs. 4.5% in 2018).
- Domestic online metrics:
  - Online revenue: $6.53B in 2019 (16.6% of Domestic revenue), up from $5.99B in 2018 and $4.84B in 2017.
  - Comparable online sales growth: 10.5% in 2019 (vs. 21.8% in 2018, 20.8% in 2017).

heading: Fiscal 2018 Results Compared With Fiscal 2017
start_phrase: Consolidated revenue of $42.2 billion in fiscal 2018 increased 7.0% compared to fiscal 2017.
summary:
- Overview of operating income trends: FY2019 operating income increased by $57 million with a flat operating margin versus FY2018, driven by a lower gross profit rate offset by a lower SG&A rate.
- FY2018 vs. FY2017 performance: Consolidated revenue rose 7.0% to $42.2 billion, including ~$760 million from an extra week. Growth drivers: +5.3% comparable sales, +1.5% non-comparable sales (net store changes, extra week, profit-share, certain credit card revenue, gift card breakage, commercial, and wholesale/dealer sales), and +0.2% FX.

- Restructuring: Charges decreased from $39 million in FY2017 to $10 million in FY2018, primarily in the Domestic segment.
- Operating income in FY2018: Decreased by $11 million; margin fell to 4.4% from 4.7%, mainly due to lower gross profit rate and higher SG&A.

  - Revenue: $36.2B (2017), $38.7B (2018, +6.7%), $39.3B (2019, +1.7%).

  - Gross profit: $8.65B → $9.07B → $9.14B; gross margin: 23.9% → 23.4% → 23.3%.
  - SG&A: $6.86B → $7.30B → $7.30B; SG&A rate: 18.9% → 18.9% → 18.6%.
  - Restructuring charges: $31M (2017), $9M (2018), $47M (2019).
  - Operating income: $1.76B (4.9%) → $1.75B (4.5%) → $1.80B (4.6%).
- Online performance (Domestic):
  - Online revenue: $4.84B (2017) → $5.99B (2018) → $6.53B (2019).
  - Online as % of segment revenue: 13.4% → 15.5% → 16.6%.

heading: Fiscal 2019 Results Compared With Fiscal 2018
start_phrase: Domestic segment revenue of $39.3 billion in fiscal 2019 increased 1.7% compared to fiscal 2018.
summary:
- Defines comparable sales, noting inclusion of comparable online sales and exclusion of the extra week in fiscal 2018.
- Reconciles Domestic segment store counts for fiscal 2017–2019: total Domestic stores fell from 1,369 (FY2017) to 1,026 (FY2019). Best Buy Mobile stand-alone stores decreased from 309 to zero following a March 1, 2018 decision to close all 257 U.S. locations, completed in Q2 FY2019. Outlet centers increased to 8; Pacific Sales declined to 21; core Best Buy stores declined to 997.
- Summarizes Domestic segment FY2019 vs FY2018 performance:
  - Revenue of $39.3B, up 1.7%. Components: +4.4% comparable sales; -2.7% non-comparable sales (reflecting the extra week in FY2018, GreatCall, and revenue streams outside the comparable base, plus a net -1.3% impact from store changes).
  - Online revenue of $6.5B, up 10.5% on a comparable basis; penetration rose to 16.6% from 15.5%.
  - Profit-share revenue from extended warranty plans was $7M in FY2019 vs $59M in FY2018, with equal impact on gross profit and operating income; decline tied to changes in premiums paid to the third-party underwriter.
  - Revenue mix and comparable sales by category (FY2019): Computing & Mobile Phones 44% (+4.2%, driven by wearables, mobile phones, computing); Consumer Electronics 33% (+3.9%, led by smart home, home theater, headphones, partially offset by digital imaging); Appliances 10% (+9.9%, large and small); Entertainment 8% (+4.7%, driven by gaming, partially offset by virtual reality); Services 5% (+7.7%, support business). Total comparable sales +4.8% (vs +5.6% in FY2018).
  - Gross profit rate declined to 23.3% from 23.4% due to higher supply chain and transportation costs and lower profit-share revenue, partially offset by better product margins (including optimization initiatives) and higher-margin mix from GreatCall.
  - SG&A decreased $4M; rate fell to 18.6% from 18.9%, driven by cost reductions, absence of the extra week, and prior-year tax reform one-time costs, partially offset by growth investments, higher variable costs from higher revenue, and GreatCall-related increases.
  - Restructuring charges were $47M in FY2019 vs $9M in FY2018, both tied to the Best Buy Mobile plan.
  - Operating income increased by $45M; operating margin was roughly flat year over year, reflecting higher gross profit offset by higher restructuring charges.
- Notes restructuring activity references to detailed disclosures in the financial statement notes.
- Provides FY2018 vs FY2017 revenue context: Domestic revenue of $38.7B, up 6.7% including ~$715M from the extra week; drivers were +5.3% comparable sales and +1.4% non-comparable sales.

title: Fiscal 2018 Results Compared With Fiscal 2017
heading: Fiscal 2018 Results Compared With Fiscal 2017
start_phrase: Domestic segment revenue of $38.7 billion in fiscal 2018 increased 6.7% compared to fiscal 2017 and includes approximately $715 million of revenue from the extra week.
summary:
- Domestic segment revenue mix and comparable sales by category for fiscal 2019 vs. 2018, and 2018 vs. 2017, showing:
  - FY2019 mix: Computing/Mobile 44%, Consumer Electronics 33%, Appliances 10%, Entertainment 8%, Services 5%; total comparable sales up 4.8% (category comps: 4.2%, 3.9%, 9.9%, 4.7%, 7.7%).
  - FY2018 mix: Computing/Mobile 45%, Consumer Electronics 33%, Appliances 10%, Entertainment 8%, Services 4%; total comparable sales up 5.6%.
  - Key drivers: wearables, mobile phones, computing; smart home, home theater, headphones; large/small appliances; gaming; services/support. Offsets from digital imaging, tablets, health/fitness, and virtual reality.
- Domestic profitability and costs:
  - FY2019 gross profit rate down to 23.3% (from 23.4%) on higher supply chain and transportation costs and lower periodic profit-share revenue; partially offset by improved product margins, gross profit optimization, and GreatCall’s higher gross margin.
  - FY2019 SG&A down $4M; rate down to 18.6% (from 18.9%) due to cost reductions and absence of extra week and prior-year tax reform costs; partially offset by growth investments, higher variable costs from increased revenue, and GreatCall acquisition.
  - Restructuring charges: $47M in FY2019 vs. $9M in FY2018, tied to the Best Buy Mobile plan.
  - Domestic operating income up $45M in FY2019 with a relatively flat operating margin; increase driven by higher gross profit, partially offset by higher restructuring.
- Domestic FY2018 vs. FY2017 highlights:
  - Revenue $38.7B, up 6.7%, including ~$715M from the extra week; components: +5.3% comparable sales and +1.4% non-comparable sales (extra week, profit-share revenue, certain credit card revenue, gift card breakage, commercial/wholesale, and net store activity of -0.7%).
  - Profit-share revenue from extended warranties: $59M in FY2018 vs. $110M in FY2017, equally benefiting gross profit and operating income; decline tied to changes in premiums to the underwriter.
  - Online revenue $6.0B, up 21.8% on a comparable basis; penetration rose to 15.5% from 13.4%.
  - Gross profit rate declined to 23.4% (from 23.9%) due to absence of $183M CRT settlement proceeds booked in FY2017 and lower profit-share revenue, partially offset by stronger category margins.
  - SG&A rate flat at 18.9%; dollar increase from higher incentive comp, growth investments, extra week, one-time tax reform costs ($75M bonuses, $20M donation), and higher variable costs; partially offset by cost reductions and nonrecurring FY2017 CRT legal fees ($22M).
  - Restructuring: $9M in FY2018 (Best Buy Mobile plan) vs. $31M in FY2017 (Renew Blue Phase 2).
  - Operating income down $12M; operating margin to 4.5% from 4.9%.
- International segment performance (Canada and Mexico):
  - Revenue: $3.575B (FY2019), $3.489B (FY2018), $3.155B (FY2017); growth of 2.5%, 10.6%, and -0.3%, respectively.
  - Comparable sales growth: 4.6% (FY2019) and 6.3% (FY2018); FY2018 included ~$45M from the extra week (excluded from comps).
  - Margins and costs: Gross profit rate 22.9% (FY2019) vs. 23.2% (FY2018) vs. 25.0% (FY2017); SG&A rate 20.0% vs. 20.6% vs. 21.9%; restructuring (benefit)/charges of $(1)M, $1M, and $8M; operating income $103M (2.9% margin) vs. $91M (2.6%) vs. $90M (2.9%).
  - 2019 revenue increase drivers: +4.4% comparable sales, partially offset by -1.9% foreign currency impact.
  - Store footprint changes: Canada Best Buy stores 134→134→132; Best Buy Mobile 53→51→45; Mexico Best Buy 20→25→29; Express 5→6→6; total International stores 212→216→212.
  - Note on Canadian brand consolidation impacting comparable sales reporting from FY2016 through most of FY2017, with comparable sales reporting resumed in Q4 FY2017.

start_phrase: International segment revenue of $3.6 billion in fiscal 2019 increased 2.5% compared to fiscal 2018.
summary:
- Excerpt from an Annual Report on Form 10-K discussing segment performance, restructuring, and financial results, with emphasis on the International segment and a brief Domestic note.
- Domestic segment: Fiscal 2018 operating income decreased $12 million year over year; operating margin fell to 4.5% from 4.9%, driven by lower gross profit rate and higher SG&A. Restructuring charges noted (with prior-year charges primarily tied to the Renew Blue Phase 2 plan); references to Note 9 for details.
- International segment three-year performance (FY2017–FY2019):
  - Revenue: $3,155m (2017), $3,489m (2018, includes ~$45m extra week), $3,575m (2019); growth of 10.6% in 2018 and 2.5% in 2019. 2019 growth driven by +4.4% comparable sales, partially offset by -1.9% FX impact.
  - Comparable sales: 6.3% in 2018; 4.6% in 2019 (International comps were suspended during/after the Canadian brand consolidation and resumed in Q4 FY2017; comps exclude the FY2018 extra week).
  - Gross profit: $790m (25.0%), $811m (23.2%), $817m (22.9%); 2019 margin decline primarily from unfavorable FX, partially offset by mix shift to higher-margin services.
  - SG&A: $692m (21.9%), $719m (20.6%), $715m (20.0%); 2019 decrease due to absence of extra week, favorable FX, and no repeat of a one-time employee bonus related to tax reform, partially offset by higher variable costs from increased sales.
  - Restructuring: $8m charges (2017), $1m charges (2018), $1m benefit (2019), tied to Canadian brand consolidation and Renew Blue, mainly adjustments to vacant space liabilities driven by sublease income estimates (see Note 9).
  - Operating income: $90m (2.9%), $91m (2.6%), $103m (2.9%); 2019 increase from higher gross profit and lower SG&A.
- International revenue mix and category comparable sales (FY2019 vs FY2018):
  - Mix: Computing & Mobile 46%; Consumer Electronics 31–32%; Appliances 8–9%; Entertainment 7%; Services 5%; Other 2%.
  - FY2019 comps: Computing & Mobile +2.7% (mobile phones, wearables); Consumer Electronics +2.0% (headphones, smart home; offset by digital imaging, home theater); Appliances +20.5% (large and small); Entertainment +1.6% (gaming; offset by movies, drones); Services +10.3% (repair); Other +30.3% (baby).

- Background on Canadian brand consolidation: closure of 66 Future Shop stores, conversion of 65 to Best Buy, and elimination of the Future Shop website materially affected comparability and reporting of International comparable sales during FY2016–Q3 FY2017.

title: Other Income (Expense)
heading: 7.4.3.1 Other Income (Expense)
start_phrase: In fiscal 2019, our gain on sale of investments was $12 million compared to $1 million and $3 million in fiscal 2018 and fiscal 2017, respectively.
summary:
- International segment: Recorded restructuring charges of $1 million in fiscal 2018 and $8 million in fiscal 2017 tied to Canadian brand consolidation and Renew Blue plans, driven by changes in sublease income estimates. Operating income was $91 million in fiscal 2018 vs. $90 million in fiscal 2017, reflecting higher gross profit and lower restructuring costs, partly offset by higher SG&A.

- Other income (expense): Gains on sale of investments were $12 million in fiscal 2019, $1 million in 2018, and $3 million in 2017, related to sales of equity investments without determinable fair values. Investment income and other increased to $49 million in 2019 from $48 million in 2018 and $31 million in 2017 due to rising U.S. interest rates and higher cash/investment balances. Interest expense remained relatively flat at $73–$75 million across fiscal 2017–2019. References provided to derivative instruments disclosure.

- Income taxes: Describes impacts of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (rate reduction from 35% to 21%, deemed repatriation tax payable over eight years) and SEC SAB 118 provisional accounting. In fiscal 2018, recorded $283 million provisional tax expense ($209 million deemed repatriation; $74 million deferred tax revaluation). In fiscal 2019, finalized calculations and reduced these amounts by $20 million and $3 million, respectively. Income tax expense fell to $424 million in 2019 (ETR 22.4%) from $818 million in 2018 (ETR 45.0%) due to the prior-year Tax Act charge and the lower statutory rate, partially offset by prior-year discrete items. Fiscal 2018 income tax expense increased from $609 million in 2017 (ETR 33.5%) mainly due to the Tax Act, partially offset by excess tax benefits from stock-based compensation, a lower blended U.S. rate (33.7%), and a higher mix of foreign pre-tax income.

- Cross-references: Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements for restructuring (Note 9), derivative instruments (Note 5), and income taxes (Note 11) within Item 8 of the Annual Report on Form 10-K.

title: Summary
heading: 7.5.1 Summary
start_phrase: We closely manage our liquidity and capital resources.
summary:
- Explains non-GAAP reconciliation items, including:
  - Acquisition-related charges for GreatCall (non-cash amortization of intangibles and transaction costs).
  - Impacts of the U.S. Tax Act (deemed repatriation, deferred tax revaluation, and related one-time employee bonus and Best Buy Foundation contribution).
  - CRT/LCD litigation settlement proceeds net of legal costs.
  - Canadian brand consolidation costs (retention and store-related, non-restructuring).
  - Gains/losses and impairments on investments recorded in investment income.
  - Tax effects of non-GAAP adjustments using U.S. and Canada statutory rates.

- Non-GAAP performance highlights:
  - Fiscal 2019 vs. 2018: operating income up $35 million on broad-based revenue strength, lower SG&A from cost reductions, and the absence of the extra week; EPS also benefited from a lower share count and tax rate.
  - Fiscal 2018 vs. 2017: operating income up $220 million; margin rose to 4.6%, driven by strong revenue and the extra week, partially offset by higher incentive compensation.

- Liquidity and capital resources overview:
  - Emphasis on disciplined capital allocation and flexibility in capex and buybacks.
  - Year-over-year decline in combined cash and short-term investments due to share repurchases, capex, the GreatCall acquisition, and dividends, partially offset by operating cash generation.

- Cash flow analysis (FY2019, FY2018, FY2017):
  - Operating activities: FY2019 improved versus FY2018 due to inventory timing and higher earnings; FY2018 declined versus FY2017 due to inventory and advertising payment timing.
  - Investing activities: FY2019 improved (fewer investment purchases) partly offset by the GreatCall acquisition; FY2018 used more cash due to higher capex and prior-year Five Star asset proceeds, partly offset by reduced net activity in short-term investments.
  - Financing activities: FY2019 outflows decreased versus FY2018 due to lower share repurchases as the $3.5B plan was reached, partly offset by higher dividends and fewer option exercises; FY2018 outflows increased versus FY2017 due to more buybacks and a higher dividend, tempered by large FY2017 outflows (debt repayment and a special dividend).

- Sources of liquidity and outlook:
  - Primary sources include operating cash flow, cash/investments, credit facilities, and other debt.
  - Management expects liquidity to fund operations, capex, buybacks, dividends, and strategic initiatives, while noting potential need to limit spending if conditions change.

- Credit facility update:
  - Entered a new $1.25 billion five-year senior unsecured revolving credit facility on April 17, 2018, expiring April 2023, replacing the prior $1.25 billion facility that was set to expire in June 2021.

start_phrase: The preparation of our financial statements requires us to make assumptions and estimates about future events and apply judgments that affect the reported amounts of assets, liabilities, revenue, expenses and the related disclosures.

title: Inventory Markdown
heading: 7.6.1 Inventory Markdown
start_phrase: Our merchandise inventories were $5.4 billion at February 2, 2019.
summary:
- The document outlines critical accounting estimates for a retail company, focusing on inventory markdowns, vendor allowances, and property and equipment impairments.
- Inventory markdowns:
  - Merchandise inventories were $5.4 billion at February 2, 2019.
  - Inventory is valued at the lower of cost or net realizable value through markdown adjustments, which set a new cost basis.
  - Estimation involves judgment about expected recovery rates influenced by product type/condition, consumer demand, product lifecycle, promotional environment, vendor return rights, sales channel, and assumptions about vendor allowances and selling costs.
  - Sensitivity: A 10% change in markdown adjustments at February 2, 2019 would have affected fiscal 2019 net earnings by approximately $11 million.
- Vendor allowances:
  - The company receives vendor funds via purchase- or sales-based volume programs and for advertising/placement.
  - Funds tied to inventory are recognized as a reduction of cost of sales when the associated inventory is sold; funds not tied to volume are recognized ratably over the promotion/placement period.
  - Reimbursements of specific, incremental, identifiable selling costs are recorded as offsets to those expenses when incurred.
  - Significant estimation/judgment is required due to diverse agreements, including classification of funding type and estimating the portion of purchases-based funding recognized in cost of sales, considering inventory turns by category and actual sell-through.
  - Sensitivity: A 10% change in vendor funding deferral at February 2, 2019 would have affected fiscal 2019 net earnings by approximately $28 million.
- Property and equipment impairments:
  - Assets are tested for impairment when events or changes in circumstances indicate potential non-recoverability.
  - First step compares carrying value to estimated undiscounted future cash flows; if not recoverable, impairment loss is measured by comparing carrying value to estimated fair value (typically based on discounted cash flows).
  - Store locations are evaluated quarterly; a primary trigger is negative store operating income over the most recent 12 months, along with changes in asset use/life or business strategies.
  - The process requires judgment in identifying triggering events and in estimating future cash flows.

title: Property and Equipment Impairments
heading: 7.6.3 Property and Equipment Impairments
start_phrase: Property and equipment assets are evaluated for impairment whenever events or changes in circumstances indicate that the carrying value may not be recoverable.
summary:
- The document outlines critical accounting estimates and related sensitivities for Best Buy, covering inventory markdowns, vendor allowances, property and equipment impairments, tax contingencies, and gift card breakage.
- Inventory markdowns: $5.4 billion of inventory at February 2, 2019 is valued at the lower of cost or net realizable value through markdown adjustments. Significant judgment is applied to expected recovery rates, vendor allowances, and selling costs. A 10% change in markdown adjustments would impact fiscal 2019 net earnings by approximately $11 million.
- Vendor allowances: Funds from vendors (purchase/sales-based programs, advertising, and placement) are recognized as reductions of cost of sales when inventory is sold, ratably over performance periods, or as offsets to related expenses if reimbursing specific costs. Complex estimates are required for classification and deferral. A 10% change in vendor funding deferral would impact net earnings by approximately $28 million.
- Property and equipment impairments: Assets are tested when indicators arise; recoverability is assessed via undiscounted cash flows, and impairments measured against estimated fair value using discounted cash flows. Stores are reviewed quarterly, with negative 12-month operating income a primary trigger. Judgments include triggers, cash flow forecasts, useful lives, and discount rates. A 10% change in non-restructuring impairments would impact net earnings by approximately $1 million.
- Tax contingencies: The company is subject to audits across jurisdictions and records liabilities for uncertain tax positions, adjusting them upon settlement, statute expirations, or new information. The effective tax rate is influenced by law changes, jurisdictional mix, earnings, and audit outcomes. Actual results could materially affect cash and the effective tax rate.
- Gift card breakage: Gift cards do not expire; revenue is recognized upon redemption and for expected breakage based on historical patterns and applicable laws, with over 90% of redemptions typically within one year. Judgments involve grouping, redemption patterns, and ultimate breakage rates. A 10% change in the cumulative estimated breakage rate would impact net earnings by approximately $51 million.

title: Tax Contingencies
heading: 7.6.4 Tax Contingencies
start_phrase: Our income tax returns are periodically audited by U.S. federal, state and local and foreign tax authorities.
summary:
- The excerpt outlines critical accounting estimates and sensitivities related to long-lived asset impairment, tax contingencies, and gift card breakage.
- Property and equipment impairment: Management forecasts future cash flows (estimated sales, margins, expenses), considers lease changes and growth rates, assesses useful lives, and selects risk-appropriate discount rates. A 10% change in non-restructuring impairment would have impacted fiscal 2019 net earnings by about $1 million.
- Tax contingencies: The company is subject to ongoing audits by U.S. federal, state, local, and foreign authorities, records liabilities for uncertain tax positions, and adjusts them upon settlement, statute expiration, or new information. The effective tax rate is influenced by law changes, jurisdictional mix of earnings, new stores/ventures, and audit outcomes. Significant judgment is required due to uncertain external (tax law changes/interpretations/timing) and internal factors (jurisdictional earnings, transaction timing, capital spending). Outcomes could materially raise or lower the effective tax rate and affect cash usage.
- Gift card breakage: Best Buy gift cards do not expire; revenue is recognized upon redemption and for estimated breakage based on historical patterns and applicable laws, aligned with redemption behavior. Over 90% of redemptions (and breakage recognition) occur within one year. Judgment is applied to card grouping, redemption patterns, and ultimate unredeemed values. A 10% change in the cumulative estimated breakage rate as of February 2, 2019 would have affected fiscal 2019 net earnings by approximately $51 million.

title: Gift Card Breakage

start_phrase: We sell Best Buy gift cards to our customers in our retail stores, online and through select third parties.
summary:

heading: Item 7A. Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk.
start_phrase:

ks inher ent in our operations, we are exposed to certain market risks.
summary:
- Service revenue accounting: Describes how revenue from bundled support plans (technical support, extended warranties, anti-virus, one-time repairs) is allocated to performance obligations based on relative standalone selling prices, often using a cost-plus approach when items are only sold in bundles. Technical support memberships are recognized over time on a usage basis informed by historical utilization; if history is insufficient, revenue is recognized ratably. Key judgments include portfolio scoping, standalone selling price estimation, and forecasting usage patterns. Sensitivity: a 10% change in services membership deferred revenue as of February 2, 2019 would have changed fiscal 2019 net earnings by about $12 million.

- Goodwill: Outlines the annual (or trigger-based) impairment testing comparing reporting units’ fair value to carrying value, using discounted cash flows and market multiples, with significant judgment in growth, expense, capex assumptions, and market comparables. Management believes Domestic reporting unit fair value significantly exceeds carrying value; GreatCall’s fair value approximately equals its carrying value, with greater uncertainty and thus higher future impairment risk. Sensitivity: a 10% change in GreatCall’s fair value at February 2, 2019 would not be material to net earnings.

- New accounting pronouncements: Directs readers to Note 1, Summary of Significant Accounting Policies, for applicable new standards.

- Market risk disclosures (Item 7A):
  - Interest rate risk: Exposure from cash/short-term investments and debt swapped to floating rates. As of February 2, 2019, $2.0 billion cash and cash equivalents and $1.2 billion of debt swapped to floating, resulting in $0.8 billion net cash exposed. A 50 bps increase in short-term rates would reduce net interest expense by ~$4 million; a 50 bps decrease would increase it by ~$4 million.
  - Foreign currency risk: Exposure from International segment (notably CAD and MXN). Use of FX forwards (generally up to 12 months) to hedge forecasted inventory purchases, recognized balances, and the Canadian net investment. FY2019 FX had an unfavorable impact of ~$68 million on revenue and ~$4 million on earnings; FY2018 FX had a favorable impact of ~$85 million on revenue and ~$4 million on earnings.

- Management’s reports (Item 8):
  - Management’s responsibility for preparing GAAP-compliant consolidated financial statements with estimates and judgments; Deloitte & Touche LLP audited the statements.
  - Internal control over financial reporting: Designed under executive oversight; assessed using COSO 2013. Management concluded controls were effective as of February 2, 2019 with no material weaknesses; Deloitte issued an unqualified attestation. Signed by the Chairman & CEO and the CFO.

title: Management's Report on the Consolidated Financial Statements
heading: Management's Report on the Consolidated Financial Statements
start_phrase: Our management is resp onsible for the preparation, integrity and objectivity of the accompanying consolidated financial statements and the related financialinformation.
summary:
- Item 8 – Financial Statements and Supplementary Data, including Management’s reports.
- Management’s Report on the Consolidated Financial Statements:
  - Management is responsible for preparation, integrity, and objectivity of the consolidated financial statements and related 10-K information.
  - Statements prepared in conformity with GAAP, incorporating estimates and judgments.
  - Deloitte & Touche LLP audited the statements under PCAOB standards and is responsible for opining on fair presentation in accordance with GAAP.
- Management’s Report on Internal Control Over Financial Reporting (ICFR):
  - Management is responsible for establishing and maintaining adequate ICFR per Exchange Act Rule 13a-15(f), designed under the CEO and CFO’s supervision.
  - ICFR aims to provide reasonable assurance of reliable reporting and GAAP-compliant financial statements through policies that:
    1) Ensure accurate, detailed records of transactions and asset dispositions.
    2) Assure transactions are recorded for GAAP reporting and that receipts/expenditures are authorized by management and the Board.
    3) Provide reasonable assurance of preventing or timely detecting unauthorized asset use/disposition that could materially affect the statements.
  - Acknowledges inherent limitations of ICFR; provides only reasonable assurance.
- ICFR assessment results:
  - Evaluated as of February 2, 2019 using COSO 2013 framework.
  - Management concluded ICFR was effective; no material weaknesses identified.
- Auditor attestation:
  - Deloitte & Touche LLP issued an unqualified attestation report on ICFR as of February 2, 2019.
- Signatories:
  - Hubert Joly, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer (principal executive officer).
  - Corie Barry, Chief Financial Officer (principal financial officer).

title: Adopted Accounting Pronouncements
heading: Adopted Accounting Pronouncements
start_phrase: In the first quarter o f fiscal 2019, we prospectively adopted the following ASUs, all of which had an immaterial impact on our results of operations, cash flows andfinancial position.
summary:
- Upcoming lease accounting change: Transition from ASC 840 to ASC 842 in fiscal 2020 with a cumulative-effect adjustment to beginning retained earnings. Company will elect the transition “package of practical expedients,” carrying forward historical lease classifications. Expected recognition of right‑of‑use assets and lease liabilities of approximately $2.6–$3.0 billion for operating leases; capital lease accounting largely unchanged. Estimated cumulative pre-tax impact will reduce retained earnings by about $20–$30 million. No material impact expected on statements of earnings or cash flows. Related control procedures and processes have been modified.

- Goodwill impairment simplification (ASU 2017-04): Eliminates Step 2; impairment measured as excess of carrying amount over fair value. Effective for fiscal years beginning after December 15, 2019. Not expected to impact consolidated financial statements; evaluation for future test impacts ongoing.

- Fair value disclosures (ASU 2018-13, Topic 820): Updates fair value measurement disclosure requirements. Effective for fiscal years and interim periods beginning after December 15, 2019. Impact under evaluation.

- Cloud computing implementation costs (ASU 2018-15, Subtopic 350-40): Apply internal-use software guidance to determine capitalization vs. expensing of implementation costs in hosting arrangements that are service contracts. Effective for fiscal years and interim periods beginning after December 15, 2019. Impact under evaluation.

- Adopted in Q1 fiscal 2019 with immaterial impact: ASU 2016-16 (Intra-Entity Transfers of Assets Other Than Inventory), ASU 2017-12 (Derivatives and Hedging), and ASU 2018-02 (Reclassification of Certain Tax Effects from AOCI).

- Revenue recognition (ASU 2014-09) adopted in Q1 fiscal 2019 using the modified retrospective method: Increased opening retained earnings by $73 million (net of tax), driven primarily by timing changes related to gift cards, certain software license sales, and loyalty programs. No restatement of prior periods; no material impact on fiscal 2019 earnings; certain control procedures modified without materially affecting ICFR.

- Quantified impacts of ASU 2014-09: On transition (Feb 4, 2018), reduced other assets by $19 million, unredeemed gift card liabilities by $69 million, deferred revenue by $26 million, increased accrued liabilities by $3 million, and increased retained earnings by $73 million. For FY ended Feb 2, 2019, relative to pre-adoption basis: revenue +$49 million, cost of goods sold +$58 million, gross profit and operating income −$9 million, income tax expense −$2 million, net earnings −$7 million, basic EPS −$0.02, diluted EPS −$0.03. Balance sheet effects as of Feb 2, 2019 include increases in other current assets (+$56 million) and accrued liabilities (+$59 million), decreases in other assets (−$19 million), unredeemed gift card liabilities (−$62 million), and deferred revenue (−$24 million), and higher retained earnings (+$64 million including opening adjustment).

- SEC disclosure update: In Q3 fiscal 2019, the SEC adopted Release No. 33-10532 (Disclosure Update and Simplification), revising certain disclosure requirements that were redundant, duplicative, outdated, or superseded.

title: Merchandise Inventories
heading: Merchandise Inventories
start_phrase: Merchandise inventories are recorded at the lower of cost or net realizable value and the weighted average method is used to determine the cost of inventory.
summary:
- Overview of accounting policy updates for interim financial statements, noting new equity reconciliation requirements had no material impact on disclosures or financials.
- Business combinations accounted for under the acquisition method: assets and liabilities recorded at fair value; excess recognized as goodwill; results included prospectively; transaction costs expensed in SG&A; reference to the fiscal 2019 acquisition of GreatCall.
- Cash, cash equivalents, and restricted cash: definitions (money market funds, commercial paper, corporate bonds, time deposits ≤3 months); balances and interest rates (cash equivalents of $1,410m at 2.5% in 2019 vs $524m at 1.1% in 2018); reconciliation of total cash, cash equivalents, and restricted cash ($2,184m in 2019; $1,300m in 2018; $2,433m in 2017); restricted cash pledged for workers’ compensation and general liability insurance.
- Receivables: primarily vendor funding, card processors, and mobile network operators; allowance based on historical collection trends; allowances of $23m (2019) and $37m (2018).
- Merchandise inventories: carried at lower of cost or net realizable value using weighted average; include inbound freight and certain vendor allowances in cost; store distribution/storage costs expensed in COGS; valuation reflects shrink estimates and markdowns to expected recovery with new cost basis and no reversals; returnable inventory to vendors not adjusted.
- Property and equipment: recorded at cost, depreciated straight-line over useful lives; leasehold improvements over shorter of useful life or lease term (including reasonably assured renewals); tax depreciation generally accelerated; disposals result in gain/loss recognition; repairs expensed, major renewals capitalized.
- Internal-use software: development costs capitalized and amortized (generally 2–7 years); enhancements capitalized if they add functionality or extend life; maintenance/training expensed; capitalized software included in fixtures and equipment.
- Property under capital and financing leases: includes buildings and equipment; depreciated over shorter of useful life or lease term; indicative useful lives: buildings 5–35 years, leasehold improvements 2–10, fixtures/equipment 2–15, leased property 3–7.
- Impairment of long-lived assets and exit activities: triggers include negative performance, strategy or usage changes; recoverability tested via undiscounted cash flows; impairments measured to fair value using discounted cash flows; assets grouped at lowest level of independent cash flows (e.g., individual stores), with separate reviews for shared assets (e.g., IT); reference to fair value measurements note for techniques and charges.
- Exit costs for vacated properties recognized at cessation of use (future lease costs net of sublease income); accelerated depreciation upon abandonment decisions; accrued obligations for vacant properties of $14m (2019) and $17m (2018).

Our inventory valuation ref

ew cost basis. No adjustment is recorded for inventory that we are able to return to our vendors for full credit. Subsequent changes infacts or circumstan
ces do not result in the reversal of previously recorded markdown adjustments or an increase in the newly established cost basis.58

title: Property and Equipment
heading: Property and Equipment
start_phrase: Property and equipment are recorded at cost.
summary:
- Property and equipment accounting policy: recorded at cost; depreciated using straight-line over estimated useful lives; leasehold improvements depreciated over the shorter of useful life or lease term (including reasonably assured renewals); accelerated methods used for tax.
- Disposals: upon retirement or disposal, remove cost and accumulated depreciation; recognize gains/losses in the income statement.
- Expenditures: routine repairs and maintenance expensed; major renewals/replacements that extend useful life capitalized and depreciated.
- Internal-use software: development/acquisition costs capitalized and amortized over 2–7 years; subsequent enhancements capitalized if they extend life or functionality; recorded in Fixtures and equipment; maintenance and training expensed.
- Leased assets: property under capital and financing leases (buildings/equipment) depreciated over the shorter of useful life or lease term.
- Estimated useful lives:
  - Buildings: 5–35 years
  - Leasehold improvements: 2–10 years
  - Fixtures and equipment: 2–15 years
  - Property under capital/financing leases: 3–7 years
- Impairment of long-lived assets: assessed when indicators arise (e.g., recent negative operating income, underperformance, changes in use/life or strategy); if undiscounted cash flows plus disposition proceeds are less than carrying value (net of other liabilities), recognize impairment and write down to fair value using discounted cash flow analysis.
- Asset grouping for impairment: evaluated at the lowest level of largely independent cash flows (e.g., individual stores); separate reviews for shared assets like IT systems; references Note 4 for valuation techniques, charges, and remaining carrying values.
- Exit activities: recognize present value of costs for vacated properties (future lease costs net of expected sublease income) when use ceases; accelerate depreciation when a decision is made to abandon property.
- Obligations for vacant properties included in accrued liabilities: $14 million at February 2, 2019; $17 million at February 3, 2018.
