title: Impairment of Long-Lived Assets and Costs Associated With Exit Activities
heading: Impairment of Long-Lived Assets and Costs Associated With Exit Activiti es
start_phrase: Long-lived assets are e valuated for impairment whenever events or changes in circumstances indicate the carrying value of an asset may not be recoverable.
summary:
- Property and equipment accounting policies: recorded at cost; straight-line depreciation over estimated useful lives; leasehold improvements depreciated over the shorter of useful life or lease term (including reasonably assured renewals); accelerated methods used for tax; disposals remove cost and accumulated depreciation with gains/losses recognized; repairs and maintenance expensed; major renewals/replacements capitalized.
- Internal-use software: development costs capitalized and amortized over 2–7 years; subsequent enhancements capitalized if they extend life or functionality; maintenance and training expensed; capitalized software presented within Fixtures and equipment.
- Capital and financing leases: assets (buildings/equipment) depreciated over the shorter of useful life or lease term (including reasonably assured renewals). Estimated useful lives: Buildings 5–35 years; Leasehold improvements 2–10; Fixtures and equipment 2–15; Property under capital/financing leases 3–7.
- Impairment of long-lived assets and exit activities: impairment testing triggered by indicators (e.g., recent negative operating income, underperformance, changes in use/life/strategy); recoverability assessed via undiscounted cash flows plus disposition proceeds; impairments measured to fair value using discounted cash flows; assets grouped at lowest independent cash-flow level (e.g., individual stores) with separate reviews for shared assets (e.g., IT). Exit costs for vacated properties (primarily future lease costs net of sublease income) recognized at present value upon cessation of use; accelerated depreciation when assets are to be retired. Obligations for vacant properties: Accrued liabilities of $14 million (2019) and $17 million (2018); Long-term liabilities of $11 million (2019) and $21 million (2018), including amounts tied to restructuring.
- Lease accounting details: majority of retail and distribution operations under leases requiring taxes, insurance, and CAM in addition to rent; many large-format store leases have <5 years remaining with renewal options; some leases include escalations and variable rent (e.g., percentage of revenue or CPI). Fixed rent escalations recognized on a straight-line basis from possession through the initial term, with differences recorded as deferred rent (in accrued or long-term liabilities). Tenant allowances recognized as a straight-line reduction of rent; unamortized balances recorded as deferred rent. Deferred rent balances: Accrued liabilities of $28 million (2019) and $30 million (2018); Long-term liabilities of $99 million (2019) and $107 million (2018). Financing leases recorded when deemed the owner (e.g., significant involvement during construction); building costs in property and equipment with related obligations in current portion of long-term debt and long-term debt; outstanding financing lease obligations of $181 million (2019) and $191 million (2018).
- Goodwill and intangible assets—goodwill: defined as purchase price in excess of fair value of identifiable net assets; impairment tested annually (first day of fiscal Q4) or upon indicators, at the reporting unit level (no aggregation). Reporting units with goodwill: Domestic and GreatCall. Quantitative impairment test compares fair value (DCF or market approaches) to carrying value; if carrying value exceeds fair value, a second step determines implied goodwill and measures impairment. For fiscal 2019 and 2018, fair values of both Domestic and GreatCall reporting units exceeded their carrying values; no goodwill impairment recorded.

title: Leases
heading: Leases
start_phrase: We conduct the majority of our retail and distribution operations from leased locations.
summary:
- Discussion of obligations related to vacant properties, including amounts recorded in long-term liabilities ($11 million at February 2, 2019, and $21 million at February 3, 2018) and reference to restructuring activities (Note 9).
- Lease arrangements for retail and distribution operations: typical lease terms, tenant responsibilities (taxes, insurance, common area maintenance), renewal options, escalation clauses, and variable rent based on sales or CPI.
- Accounting policies for leases: straight-line recognition of rent for fixed escalations from property possession through initial term; treatment of deferred rent; recognition of tenant allowances as a reduction to rent on a straight-line basis and inclusion of unamortized portions in deferred rent.
- Reported deferred rent balances: $28 million and $30 million in accrued liabilities, and $99 million and $107 million in long-term liabilities at February 2, 2019, and February 3, 2018, respectively.
- Financing lease arrangements (including build-to-suit/sale-leaseback-type situations where the company is deemed the owner): recognition of building cost in property and equipment with corresponding liabilities in current and long-term debt; outstanding financing lease obligations of $181 million (2019) and $191 million (2018); cross-reference to Note 10 for maturities.
- Depreciation policy for assets under capital and financing leases: over the shorter of useful life or lease term, including reasonably assured renewal periods.
- Goodwill and intangible assets—goodwill: definition, annual impairment testing timing (first day of fiscal Q4) and triggering events, reporting unit determination (no aggregation), and methodology (quantitative assessment using discounted cash flows and market approaches; two-step process if carrying value exceeds fair value).
- Reporting units with goodwill: Domestic and GreatCall; conclusion that no goodwill impairment was recorded in fiscal 2019 and 2018 as fair values exceeded carrying values.

title: Goodwill
heading: Goodwill
start_phrase: Goodwill is the excess of the purch ase price over the fair value of identifiable net assets acquired in business combinations.
summary:
- Overview of lease-related accounting and obligations:
  - Majority of retail and distribution facilities are leased; leases often require taxes, insurance, and common area maintenance in addition to rent; many large-format store leases have less than 5 years remaining with renewal options; some leases include rent escalations and variable rent tied to revenue or CPI.
  - Rent with fixed escalations is recognized on a straight-line basis from possession through the initial term; differences recorded as deferred rent in accrued or long-term liabilities.
  - Tenant allowances are recognized as a straight-line reduction to rent over the initial lease term; unamortized balances recorded as deferred rent.
  - Deferred rent balances: $28 million (accrued) and $99 million (long-term) at Feb 2, 2019; $30 million (accrued) and $107 million (long-term) at Feb 3, 2018.
  - Financing leases recorded when the company is deemed the owner (e.g., significant construction involvement); building costs recorded in property and equipment; liabilities recorded in current portion and long-term debt; outstanding financing lease obligations of $181 million (2019) and $191 million (2018). Assets under capital/financing leases are depreciated over the shorter of useful life or lease term (including reasonably assured renewals).
  - Obligations associated with vacant properties included in long-term liabilities were $11 million (2019) and $21 million (2018), including amounts tied to restructuring (see Note 9).

- Goodwill:
  - Goodwill impairment testing performed annually (first day of fiscal Q4) or upon indicators; evaluated at the reporting unit level (Domestic and GreatCall).
  - Quantitative testing compares fair value (DCF/market approaches) to carrying value; if necessary, a second step estimates implied fair value of goodwill.
  - No goodwill impairments recorded for Domestic in fiscal 2019 and 2018; no impairment for GreatCall in fiscal 2019.
  - Goodwill carrying value: $915 million (2019) vs. $425 million (2018). Gross carrying amount and cumulative impairment: $1,590 million gross with $675 million cumulative impairment (2019); $1,100 million gross with $675 million cumulative impairment (2018).

- Indefinite-lived intangible assets:
  - Pacific Sales tradename (Domestic segment) recorded in Other assets; tested annually using the relief-from-royalty method; no impairments in fiscal 2019 or 2018.
  - Carrying value of tradename: $18 million at both Feb 2, 2019, and Feb 3, 2018.

- Definite-lived intangible assets (GreatCall, within Domestic segment):
  - As of Feb 2, 2019: gross carrying amounts and accumulated amortization—Customer relationships $258m/$16m; Tradename $63m/$3m; Developed technology $52m/$4m; total $373m gross, $23m accumulated. No definite-lived intangibles as of Feb 3, 2018.
  - Expected amortization expense: 2020 $68m; 2021 $68m; 2022 $67m; 2023 $67m; 2024 $48m; thereafter $32m.

- Insurance:
  - Self-insured for workers’ compensation, medical, and general liability with third-party excess coverage; some risks managed via a wholly owned captive.
  - Liabilities include reported claims and IBNR; estimates informed by independent third-party actuarial valuations.

title: Income Taxes
heading: Income Taxes
start_phrase: We account for income taxes using the asset and liability method.
summary:
- Self-insurance: Company uses internal insurance/risk expertise alongside external coverage; self-insured liabilities recorded on the Consolidated Balance Sheets totaled $129 million at February 2, 2019 (comprised of $69 million in accrued liabilities and $60 million in long-term liabilities) versus $131 million at February 3, 2018 ($67 million accrued, $64 million long-term).
- Income taxes: Applies the asset-and-liability method, recognizing deferred tax assets/liabilities for basis differences and carryforwards, with valuation allowances as needed. Uses an annual effective tax rate reflecting permanent differences, statutory rates, and audit outcomes, updated as new information arises. Discrete events (e.g., audit settlements, law changes) are recognized in the period incurred. Returns are audited by U.S. federal, state/local, and foreign authorities; liabilities for unrecognized tax benefits (including penalties and interest) are recorded in Long-term liabilities and related expense in Income tax expense, and adjusted upon settlement, statute expiration, or new information.
- Accrued liabilities: Key components include non-income tax liabilities, advertising accruals, income tax accruals, loyalty program liabilities, rent-related liabilities, and sales return reserves.
- Long-term liabilities: Key components include unrecognized tax benefits, income tax liabilities, rent-related liabilities, and self-insurance reserves.
- Foreign currency: Assets and liabilities translated at period-end (or one-month-lagged) exchange rates; results and cash flows at average rates. Translation effects recorded in accumulated other comprehensive income; transaction gains/losses included in SG&A and not significant in presented periods.
- Revenue recognition: Revenue primarily from product and service sales (as principal and agent), recognized upon transfer of control in amounts reflecting expected consideration. Reported net of sales and usage-based taxes and net of expected refunds (returns and cancellations), with corresponding reductions to cost of sales.

title: Credit Card Revenue
heading: Credit Card Revenue
start_phrase: We offer promotional financing and credit cards issued by third-party banks that manage and directly extend credit to our customers.
summary:
- Describes revenue recognition policies for variable consideration tied to performance-based profit-sharing and commissions.
- Extended warranties: Company earns service and commission revenues from warranty sales, including a profit-share that is a form of variable consideration. Profit-share is recognized as revenue using the expected value method once annual claims experience is known, typically in the fiscal fourth quarter, with payment in the subsequent fiscal year. Warranty-related service and commission revenues were 2.0%, 2.0%, and 2.2% of revenue in fiscal 2019, 2018, and 2017, including profit-share of $10 million, $68 million, and $133 million, respectively.
- Mobile carrier commissions: Fixed activation commissions are recognized at a point in time upon contract sale and customer activation. Cash collection generally occurs 30–60 days after activation. Commissions are subject to clawback for customer cancellations; revenue is recorded net of expected cancellations based on historical rates.
- Credit card programs: Third-party banks issue promotional financing and credit cards; the company licenses its brand and facilitates applications, acts as an agent, and holds no customer receivables. The company earns a profit-share from certain banking partners based on annual program performance, with quarterly payments. This variable consideration is recognized over time using the most likely amount method when a significant revenue reversal is not probable, typically assessed quarterly.
- Gift cards: Revenue is recognized upon redemption. Breakage is recognized based on historical redemption patterns and applicable laws, using a method consistent with redemption behavior; over 90% of redemptions (and breakage recognition) occur within one year of issuance. Breakage income was $34 million, $40 million, and $37 million in fiscal 2019, 2018, and 2017, respectively. Judgment applies to grouping, redemption patterns, and ultimate unredeemed values.
- Sales incentives: Incentives earned only with a purchase (e.g., a gift card at purchase or future-use coupon) are treated as a material right and a separate performance obligation. The relative standalone selling price is deferred as a contract liability based on projected redemptions and recognized when redeemed or when not expected to be redeemed, with judgment in grouping, redemption patterns, and expected non-redemptions. Coupons not earned with a purchase (e.g., targeted marketing) are not a performance obligation and reduce the transaction price when redeemed.

akage revenue) occur within one year of issuance. There is judgment in assessing (1) the level at which we group gift cards for analysis ofbreakage rates, (2) r

title: Sales Incentives
heading: Sales Incentives
start_phrase: We frequently offer sales ince ntives that entitle our customers to receive a gift card at the time of purchase or an instant savings coupon that can be redeemedtowards a future purchase.
summary:
- Revenue recognition for extended warranties and related profit-share arrangements:
  - Profit-share is variable consideration based on portfolio profitability; Best Buy does not share in portfolio losses.
  - Recognized using the expected value method when annual claims experience is known (typically fiscal Q4); cash received the following fiscal year.
  - Service and commission revenues from extended warranties were 2.0%, 2.0%, and 2.2% of revenue in fiscal 2019, 2018, and 2017, including profit-share of $10M, $68M, and $133M, respectively.

- Commissions from mobile network carriers:
  - Fixed commissions for selling/activating service contracts recognized at a point in time upon customer activation.
  - Payments generally received within 30–60 days post-activation.
  - Commissions subject to chargebacks for cancellations; revenue reported net of expected cancellations based on historical rates.

- Credit card revenue (promotional financing and co-branded cards):
  - Programs run by third-party banks; Best Buy acts as agent and does not hold receivables.
  - Eligible for profit-share based on annual program performance; variable consideration recognized over time using the most likely amount when a significant reversal is not probable; payments occur quarterly.

- Gift cards:
  - No expiration; revenue recognized upon redemption.
  - Breakage recognized consistent with redemption patterns based on historical data and jurisdictional rules; over 90% of redemptions (and breakage recognition) occur within one year.
  - Breakage income: $34M (fiscal 2019), $40M (2018), $37M (2017).

- Sales incentives:
  - Incentives earned with a purchase (e.g., gift cards at purchase, future-use coupons) are material rights and separate performance obligations.
  - Relative standalone selling price deferred as a contract liability based on projected redemptions; revenue recognized when redeemed or when redemption is not expected.
  - Coupons not earned with a purchase (marketing offers) reduce the transaction price when redeemed.
  - Significant judgment in grouping incentives, estimating redemption patterns, and expected breakage.

- Customer loyalty programs:
  - Points earned on purchases or via co-branded cards create material rights/performance obligations.
  - Standalone selling price of points deferred in accrued liabilities based on projected redemptions; revenue recognized over time as certificates are estimated to be redeemed.
  - Certificates typically expire 2–12 months after issuance; estimates rely on historical redemption data.

- Expense classification:
  - Cost of Goods Sold includes product costs; inbound and inter-facility freight; vendor allowances not tied to specific, incremental, identifiable costs; cash discounts; services-related payroll/parts; inventory losses; markdowns; customer shipping/handling; distribution network operating costs and depreciation.
  - Selling, General and Administrative includes payroll/benefits for retail and corporate; occupancy/maintenance; depreciation/amortization; advertising; vendor allowances that reimburse specific, incremental, identifiable costs; tender costs (bank charges, interchange fees); charitable contributions; outside/outsourced services; long-lived asset impairments; and other admin costs (supplies, travel, lodging).

- Vendor allowances:
  - Funds from vendors (volume-based, advertising, product placement) generally recorded as a reduction of cost of sales when associated inventory is sold.
  - If not tied to purchase/sales volumes, recognized ratably over the promotional performance period.

title: Fair Value Measurements - Introduction
heading: 4. Fair Value Measurements
start_phrase: Fair value is the price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability (an exit price) in the principal or most advantageous market for the assetor liability in an orderly transaction between market participants on the measurement date.
summary: Defines fair value as the exit price to sell an asset or transfer a liability in the principal or most advantageous market in an orderly transaction between market participants on the measurement date, and outlines a three-tier valuation hierarchy based on input observability: Level 1 (unadjusted quoted prices in active markets for identical items), Level 2 (significant other observable inputs, including quoted prices for similar assets in active markets, quoted prices for identical or similar assets in inactive markets, other observable inputs, and inputs derived from or corroborated by observable market data), and Level 3 (significant unobservable inputs requiring management judgment and pricing models using management’s estimates of market participant assumptions).
text:
Fair Value Measurements
Fair value is the price 
that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability (an exit price) in the principal or most advantageous market for the assetor liability in an orderly
 transaction between market participants on the measurement date. To measure fair value, we use a three-tier valuation hierarchy basedupon observable and non-observable 
inputs: 
Level 1 
— Unadjusted quoted prices that are available in active markets for the identical assets or liabilities at the measurement date. 
Level 2 
— Significant other observable inputs available at the measurement date, other than quoted prices included in Level 1, either directly or indirectly,including:
 
•
Quoted prices for similar assets or liabilities in active markets;•
Quoted prices for identical or similar assets or liabilities in non-active markets;•
Inputs other than quoted prices that are observable for the asset or liability; and•
Inputs that are derived principally from or corroborated by other observable market data. 
Level 3 
— Significant unobservable inputs that cannot be corroborated by observable market data and reflect the use of significant management judgment. Thesevalues are generally d
etermined using pricing models for which the assumptions utilize management’s estimates of market participant assumptions.

summary:
- Intangible assets: Adjusted fair values and amortization lives identified, including consumer customer relationships ($235 million, 5 years), tradename ($63 million, 8 years), developed technology ($52 million, 5 years), and commercial customer relationships ($23 million, 10 years). Measurement period adjustments finalized the working capital adjustment.
- Discontinued operations: Activity relates to the International segment. Fiscal 2018 primarily reflects non-compete proceeds from the sale of Best Buy Europe to Carphone Warehouse plc; fiscal 2017 reflects sales of remaining Five Star property assets; fiscal 2019 had no discontinued operations. Reported net earnings from discontinued operations were $1 million (2018) and $21 million (2017).
- Fair value framework: Definition of fair value and the three-level hierarchy (Levels 1–3), with emphasis on using the lowest significant input and management judgment where applicable.
- Recurring fair value measurements: Breakdown of assets and liabilities by hierarchy level at February 2, 2019 and February 3, 2018, including:
  - Level 1: Money market funds; marketable securities funding deferred compensation.
  - Level 2: Commercial paper, time deposits, foreign currency derivatives, and interest rate swap derivatives (both assets and liabilities).
- Valuation methods and assumptions:
  - Money market funds measured via quoted market prices (Level 1).
  - Commercial paper and time deposits measured using observable inputs; time deposits approximated by face value plus accrued interest (Level 2).
  - Foreign currency derivatives valued using observable market data (e.g., forward points, interest rates) (Level 2).
  - Deferred compensation assets tied to mutual fund performance (Level 1).
  - Interest rate swaps valued using observable interest rate inputs (e.g., LIBOR) (Level 2).
- Nonrecurring fair value measurements: Impairments recorded for property and equipment in fiscal 2019 and fiscal 2018 (including a restructuring-related impairment in 2018). Measurements used Level 3 inputs, primarily discounted cash flow models with forecasts and discount rates; for restructuring-related assets, no future cash flows were assumed and expected sale values were nominal.
- Other financial instruments: Cash, receivables, accounts payable, and other payables approximate carrying value (would be Level 1 if measured at fair value). Other investments held at cost approximate fair value. Long-term debt fair value referenced elsewhere.
- Derivative instruments and hedging: Use of foreign currency derivatives and interest rate swaps to manage exchange rate and interest rate risk; not used for trading or speculation. Counterparties are investment-grade. Derivatives are recorded at fair value, with hedge effectiveness assessed and formal hedge documentation maintained.

title: Assets and Liabilities Measured at Fair Value on a Nonrecurring Basis
heading: Assets and Liabilities Measured at Fa ir Value on a Nonrecurring Basis
start_phrase: Assets and liabilities th at are measured at fair value on a nonrecurring basis relate primarily to our tangible fixed assets, goodwill and other intangible assets, whichare remeasured when the d erived fair value is below carrying value on our Consolidated Balance Sheets.
summary:
- Fair value hierarchy and classifications:
  - Certain mutual fund investments are Level 1 due to active trading and readily available pricing.
  - Interest rate swap derivatives are measured at fair value using observable inputs (e.g., LIBOR) and classified as Level 2 because they are custom OTC contracts.

- Nonrecurring fair value measurements and impairments:
  - Long‑lived assets (property and equipment), goodwill, and other intangibles are remeasured to fair value only upon impairment; otherwise carried at cost.
  - Impairment losses are recorded in SG&A (non‑restructuring) or Restructuring charges, as applicable.
  - A table summarizes impairment charges and remaining net carrying values for fiscal 2019 and 2018 for continuing operations; remaining carrying values approximate fair value and may reflect earlier measurement dates.

- Valuation methodology for impairments (Level 3):
  - Fair values determined primarily via discounted cash flow models using forecasts of revenues, expenses, significant cash outflows (e.g., capex), and an appropriate discount rate.
  - For restructuring‑related assets assumed to cease use, no future cash flows are assumed and expected sale values are nominal.

- Fair value of other financial instruments:
  - Cash, receivables, accounts payable, and other payables approximate carrying value due to short‑term nature and would be Level 1 if measured at fair value.
  - Other cost‑method investments are estimated to approximate fair value.
  - Long‑term debt fair value is discussed separately (see Note 6).

- Derivative instruments and hedge accounting:
  - The company uses foreign currency derivatives and interest rate swaps to manage exposure to FX and interest rate risk; not used for trading or speculation.
  - All derivatives are recorded on the balance sheet at fair value; hedge effectiveness is evaluated when hedge accounting is elected, with formal documentation of hedging relationships.
  - Counterparty credit risk is mitigated by transacting with investment‑grade financial institutions; no derivatives contain credit risk‑related contingent features.

title: Derivative Instruments - Introduction
heading: 5. Derivative Instruments
start_phrase: We manage our economic and transaction exposure to certain risks by using foreign currency derivative instruments and interest rate swaps.
summary: Describes the company’s use of foreign currency derivatives and interest rate swaps to manage economic and transactional exposure to foreign exchange and interest rate risks, aiming to reduce volatility in net earnings, cash flows, and net asset value. States derivatives are not held for trading or speculation, have no credit risk–related contingent features, and counterparty credit risk is mitigated by using investment‑grade financial institutions. All derivatives are recorded at fair value on the Consolidated Balance Sheets, with hedge effectiveness assessed prospectively or retrospectively when hedge accounting is applied. Hedging relationships, underlying items, and risk management objectives are formally documented at inception, and some derivatives are not designated as hedging instruments.

title: Net Investment Hedges
heading: Net Investment Hedges
start_phrase: We use foreign exchange fo rward contracts to hedge against the effect of Canadian dollar exchange rate fluctuations on a portion of our net investment in ourCanadian operations.
summary:
- Overview of the company’s derivative and hedge accounting framework, including documentation at inception, identification of hedged items, and risk management objectives and strategies. Notes that some derivatives are not designated as hedging instruments.
- Net investment hedges:
  - Use of foreign exchange forward contracts to hedge Canadian dollar exposure on a portion of the company’s net investment in Canadian operations, with terms up to 12 months.
  - Accounting: changes in fair value recognized in other comprehensive income (OCI) as a component of foreign currency translation to offset changes in the translated value of the net investment; amounts reclassified to earnings only upon complete or substantially complete liquidation of the investment.
  - Amounts excluded from hedge effectiveness are recognized in net earnings.
- Interest rate swaps:
  - “Receive fixed, pay variable” swaps used to mitigate interest rate fluctuations on fixed-rate debt (previously 2018 Notes; currently 2021 and 2028 Notes).
  - Designated as fair value hedges using the shortcut method because critical terms and notionals match the hedged debt; changes in derivative fair value offset by adjustments to the carrying value of the debt, resulting in no impact on earnings from fair value changes.
- Derivatives not designated as hedging instruments:
  - Foreign currency forwards used to manage FX risk on recognized receivables and payables in non-functional currencies, generally with terms up to 12 months.
  - Gains and losses recognized directly in net earnings.
- Summary of derivative balances (fair values):
  - Assets at Feb 2, 2019 vs. Feb 3, 2018: $26 million vs. $2 million, driven by interest rate swaps ($26 million in other assets in 2019; none in 2018). Net investment hedge asset declined to $0 from $2 million.
  - Liabilities at Feb 2, 2019 vs. Feb 3, 2018: $1 million vs. $13 million, including interest rate swaps ($1 million vs. $5 million), net investment hedges ($0 vs. $7 million), and non-designated FX forwards ($0 vs. $1 million).
- Effects on OCI for derivatives designated as net investment hedges:
  - 2019: pre-tax gain of $21 million.
  - 2018: pre-tax loss of $14 million.

title: Interest Rate Swaps
heading: Interest Rate Swaps
start_phrase: We utilized "receive fixed-rate, pa y variable-rate" interest rate swaps to mitigate the effect of interest rate fluctuations on our 2018 Notes, prior to their maturity,and currently have swaps outstand ing on our 2021 Notes and 2028 Notes.
summary:
- Focus: Company’s use of derivatives and hedge accounting, including documentation at inception, risk management objectives/strategies, and treatment of derivatives both designated and not designated as hedges.
- Net investment hedges: Use of foreign exchange forward contracts (terms up to 12 months) to hedge Canadian dollar exposure on a portion of net investment in Canadian operations. Changes in fair value recorded in other comprehensive income (OCI) within foreign currency translation to offset changes in the net investment; amounts reclassified to earnings only upon complete or substantially complete liquidation. Amounts excluded from hedge effectiveness are recognized in net earnings. Reported pre-tax OCI impact: $21 gain in 2019 vs. $(14) loss in 2018.
- Interest rate swaps: “Receive fixed, pay variable” swaps used to hedge fixed-rate debt (prior 2018 Notes; currently 2021 and 2028 Notes). Designated as fair value hedges under the shortcut method due to matching critical terms and notional amounts. Accounting: changes in derivative fair value offset by changes to carrying value of the hedged debt; no impact on Consolidated Statements of Earnings from these fair value changes.
- Derivatives not designated as hedging instruments: Foreign currency forward contracts used to manage FX risk on recognized receivables and payables in non-functional currencies (terms up to 12 months). Gains and losses recognized directly in net earnings.
- Summary of derivative balances (fair values and balance sheet classification):
  - Assets at Feb 2, 2019: $26 million in Other assets (interest rate swaps); $0 for net investment hedges. At Feb 3, 2018: $2 million in Other current assets (net investment hedges); $0 for interest rate swaps.
  - Liabilities at Feb 2, 2019: $1 million for interest rate swaps (accrued and long-term); $0 for net investment hedges and non-designated FX forwards. At Feb 3, 2018: $7 million for net investment hedges (accrued liabilities), $5 million for interest rate swaps (accrued and long-term), and $1 million for non-designated FX forwards (accrued liabilities).
  - Totals: Assets $26 (2019) vs. $2 (2018); Liabilities $1 (2019) vs. $13 (2018).
- Presentation: Effects of net investment hedge derivatives on OCI are disclosed for fiscal 2019 and 2018.
text:
Interest Rate Swaps
We utilized "receive fixed-rate, pa
y variable-rate" interest rate swaps to mitigate the effect of interest rate fluctuations on our 2018 Notes, prior to their maturity,and currently have swaps outstand
ing on our 2021 Notes and 2028 Notes. Our interest rate swap contracts are considered perfect hedges because the critical termsand notional amounts match 
those of our fixed-rate debt being hedged and are, therefore, accounted for as fair value hedges using the shortcut method. Under theshortcut method, we recogniz
e the change in the fair value of the derivatives with an offsetting change to the carrying value of the debt. Accordingly, there is noimpact on our Consolidated Stat
ements of Earnings from the fair value of the derivatives.

heading: Derivatives Not Designated as Hedging Instrumen ts

summary:
- Describes the company’s use of derivatives and hedging strategies, including required hedge documentation, objectives, and risk management approach.
- Net investment hedges: Uses foreign exchange forward contracts (terms up to 12 months) to hedge Canadian dollar exposure on its Canadian net investment. Changes in fair value are recorded in other comprehensive income (OCI) as foreign currency translation; amounts are reclassified to net earnings only upon complete or substantially complete liquidation of the investment. Any amounts excluded from hedge effectiveness are recognized in net earnings.
- Interest rate swaps: Employs receive-fixed, pay-variable swaps to hedge fixed-rate debt (previously 2018 Notes; currently 2021 and 2028 Notes). These are accounted for as fair value hedges using the shortcut method because critical terms match the hedged debt; changes in derivative fair value are offset by adjustments to the carrying value of the debt, resulting in no impact on earnings from these fair value changes.
- Derivatives not designated as hedges: Uses short-dated (up to 12 months) FX forwards to manage non-functional currency receivables and payables; gains and losses are recognized directly in net earnings.
- Summary of derivative balances (fair values): At February 2, 2019 versus February 3, 2018, assets totaled $26 million vs. $2 million (primarily interest rate swaps in other assets), and liabilities totaled $1 million vs. $13 million (declines in net investment hedge and interest rate swap liabilities; no hedge designation FX forwards declined to zero).

title: Summary of Derivative Balances
heading: Summary of Derivative Balances
start_phrase: The following table presents the gross fair values of our outstanding derivative instruments and the corresponding classification at February 2, 2019 , and February 3, 2018 ($ in millions):
summary:
- Overview of derivative and hedging activities:
  - Net investment hedges: Use of foreign exchange forward contracts to hedge Canadian net investment; changes in fair value recorded in OCI as foreign currency translation, with reclassification to earnings only upon complete or substantial liquidation; excluded components recognized in earnings; contract terms up to 12 months.
  - Interest rate swaps: “Receive fixed, pay variable” swaps used to hedge fixed-rate notes (2018, 2021, 2028); designated as fair value hedges under the shortcut method with matching critical terms; derivative fair value changes offset adjustments to debt carrying value, resulting in no net impact on earnings.
  - Derivatives not designated as hedges: FX forwards used to manage transactional exposures on non-functional currency receivables/payables; gains and losses recognized directly in net earnings; terms up to 12 months.

- Derivative balances and results:
  - Fair value of derivatives at year-end:
    - Assets: $26m (2019) vs $2m (2018), primarily interest rate swaps.
    - Liabilities: $1m (2019) vs $13m (2018), including swaps and FX forwards.
  - OCI impact from net investment hedges: Pre-tax gain of $21m (2019) vs loss of $(14)m (2018).
  - Earnings impact of non-designated FX forwards (SG&A): Gain of $4m (2019) vs loss of $(3)m (2018).
  - Fair value hedge accounting effects (interest expense): Swap gains/(losses) of $31m/$(18)m offset by equal and opposite adjustments to debt carrying value, yielding zero net P&L effect in both years.

- Notional amounts outstanding:
  - Net investment hedges: $15m (2019) vs $462m (2018).
  - Interest rate swaps: $1,150m in both 2019 and 2018.
  - Non-designated FX forwards: $9m (2019) vs $33m (2018).
  - Total notionals: $1,174m (2019) vs $1,645m (2018).

- Debt—Short-term financing:
  - U.S. Revolving Credit Facility: New $1.25 billion five-year senior unsecured revolver entered April 17, 2018 (replacing prior $1.25b facility); expires April 2023; no borrowings outstanding at Feb 2, 2019 or Feb 3, 2018.
  - Pricing: Variable rate—either ABR (based on the greatest of prime, fed funds/overnight bank funding rate + 0.5%, or 1-month LIBOR + 1%) plus ABR margin (0.00%–0.30%), or LIBOR plus LIBOR margin (0.80%–1.30%); facility fee 0.08%–0.20%; all tiered by senior unsecured rating.
  - Covenants/guarantees: Guaranteed by certain subsidiaries; customary covenants limiting liens, structural/business changes, material asset disposals, mergers, and affiliate transactions; financial covenants include maximum quarterly cash flow leverage and minimum quarterly interest coverage; standard default provisions.

title: U.S. Revolving Credit Facility
heading: U.S. Revolving Credit Facility
start_phrase: On April 17, 2018, we entered into a $1.25 billion five-year senior unsecured revolving credit facility agreement (the "Five-Year Facility Agreement") with a syndicate of banks.
summary:
- Derivatives and hedging:
  - Effects of derivatives not designated as hedges: foreign exchange contracts impacted SG&A with a $4 million gain in fiscal 2019 and a $3 million loss in fiscal 2018.
  - Interest rate derivatives and debt valuation adjustments: interest rate swap contracts recognized in interest expense showed a $31 million gain in 2019 and an $18 million loss in 2018, offset by equal and opposite adjustments to the carrying value of long-term debt, resulting in no net impact in either year.
  - Notional amounts at February 2, 2019 vs. February 3, 2018 (in millions): net investment hedges $15 vs. $462; interest rate swaps $1,150 vs. $1,150; non-designated FX forwards $9 vs. $33; total $1,174 vs. $1,645.

- Debt:
  - Revolving credit facility: New $1.25 billion five-year senior unsecured facility entered April 17, 2018 (replacing a prior facility), expiring April 2023; no borrowings outstanding at fiscal year-end. Variable interest based on ABR or LIBOR plus a margin tied to credit ratings (ABR margin 0.00%–0.30%; LIBOR margin 0.80%–1.30%; facility fee 0.08%–0.20%). Guaranteed by certain subsidiaries and includes customary covenants (limits on liens, structural changes, asset dispositions, mergers, affiliate transactions) and financial tests (maximum leverage, minimum interest coverage). Company was in compliance as of February 2, 2019.
  - Long-term debt composition (in millions): 2018 Notes $0 (vs. $500 prior year), 2021 Notes $650, 2028 Notes $500, interest rate swap valuation adjustments $25 (vs. $(5)$), subtotal $1,175 (vs. $1,145); less discounts/issuance costs $(7)$ (vs. $(3)$); financing lease obligations $181 (vs. $191); capital lease obligations $39 (vs. $22). Total long-term debt $1,388 (vs. $1,355); current portion $56 (vs. $544); long-term portion $1,332 (vs. $811).
  - 2018 Notes: $500 million due August 1, 2018 repaid using cash; previously classified as current.
  - 2021 Notes: $650 million due March 15, 2021; 5.50% fixed, semiannual interest; issued at slight discount with $644 million net proceeds; make-whole redemption, 101% change-of-control put; unsecured and unsubordinated; covenants limiting secured debt and sale-leasebacks.
  - 2028 Notes: $500 million due October 1, 2028; 4.45% fixed, semiannual interest; $495 million net proceeds; make-whole redemption and change-of-control provisions similar to 2021 Notes.

heading: 8. Revenue Recognition
start_phrase: We generate revenue p rimarily from the sale of products and services, both as a principal and as an agent.
summary:
- Share repurchases: Detailed disclosure of common stock repurchases and retirements for fiscal 2019, 2018, and 2017, including total cost, average price per share, and number of shares; references to a January 2016 accelerated share repurchase (ASR); note that repurchased shares are retired and become authorized but unissued; additional repurchases after fiscal year-end.
- Comprehensive income: Reconciliation of accumulated other comprehensive income (AOCI) driven primarily by foreign currency translation adjustments from 2016 through 2019; note that no income tax is provided on indefinitely reinvested foreign earnings.
- Revenue recognition (ASC 606): Policies for recognizing revenue as principal and agent based on transfer of control; handling of variable consideration; refund estimates and related liabilities/assets (with noted increases from adopting new guidance); treatment of multiple performance obligations and allocation using standalone selling prices; balances and movements in deferred revenue and other contract liabilities; typical contract durations and lack of material contract assets.
- Contract balances and credit risk: Tables for receivables (net of allowance), short- and long-term contract liabilities (gift cards, deferred revenue, accrued liabilities), and a rollforward of the allowance for doubtful accounts for fiscal 2019.
- Contract liability rollforward and future revenue: Revenue recognized from opening contract liabilities, increases from the GreatCall acquisition, and adjustments; schedule of revenue expected to be recognized beyond one year (2020–2023); use of practical expedient to expense incremental costs of obtaining contracts with amortization periods of one year or less.
- Segment disclosure reference: Pointer to disaggregation of revenue by reportable segment and product category in a separate note.
- Restructuring charges: Summary of charges by program for fiscal 2019, 2018, and 2017, including Best Buy Mobile, Renew Blue (and Phase 2), and Canadian brand consolidation; detailed explanation of the 2019 plan to close all remaining 257 U.S. Best Buy Mobile stand-alone stores, rationale, timing of closures, and classification within continuing operations of the Domestic segment.

title: Tax Reform
heading: Tax Reform
start_phrase: On December 22, 2017, the U.S. enacted the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (“Tax Act”), which significantly changed U.S. tax law.
summary:
- Lease commitments: Detailed schedule of future minimum payments by fiscal year for capital, financing, and operating leases as of February 2, 2019, including totals and present values. Notes that operating lease obligations exclude landlord charges for real estate taxes and common area maintenance (which would add $0.8 billion) and are not reduced for approximately $71 million of future sublease income.
- Income tax expense and rates: Reconciliation of statutory to effective tax rates for fiscal 2019, 2018, and 2017 with effective rates of 22.4%, 45.0%, and 33.5%, respectively. Components include state taxes, foreign operations impact, other items, and the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA).
- TCJA impacts: Description of the 2017 U.S. tax reform (rate cut to 21%, deemed repatriation tax, base broadening) and SAB 118 provisional accounting. Fiscal 2018 included $283 million of provisional tax expense ($209 million deemed repatriation, $74 million deferred tax revaluation). In fiscal 2019, finalized adjustments reduced the repatriation tax by $20 million (final $189 million) and reduced the revaluation charge by $3 million (net $71 million). Election to treat GILTI as a current period expense and a refined assertion on indefinite reinvestment of certain foreign earnings.
- Earnings mix: Pre-tax earnings by jurisdiction for fiscal 2019–2017, showing the U.S. as the primary source with a consistent foreign contribution.
- Tax provision detail: Breakdown of current and deferred income tax expense by federal, state, and foreign for fiscal 2019–2017.
- Deferred taxes: Composition of deferred tax assets and liabilities as of February 2, 2019, and February 3, 2018; net deferred tax asset declined year over year and is reported in Other assets.
- Tax attributes and valuation allowance: Summary of net operating loss, credit, and capital loss carryforwards (various expirations and some with no expiration). Valuation allowance of $91 million at February 2, 2019, with explanations for changes from the prior year and allocation across U.S. and international attributes.
- Unrecognized tax benefits: Rollforward for fiscal 2019–2017; amounts that would favorably affect the effective tax rate if recognized; treatment of interest and penalties, amounts accrued, and audit status. Note that changes over the next 12 months are reasonably possible but not expected to be material.

Non-qualified deferred compensation plan for executives and directors; related liability and corresponding investment assets used to economically hedge the obligation.
- Contingencies and commitments: General disclosure of legal proceedings and accrual approach, with specific mention of long-running securities class actions filed in 2011 alleging Exchange Act violations related to fiscal 2011 guidance, later consolidated in federal court.
text:
Tax Reform
On December 22, 2017, the U.S. enacted the Tax Cuts 
and Jobs Act (“Tax Act”), which significantly changed U.S. tax law. Among other things, the Tax Actlowered the U.S. statutory tax ra
te from 35%  to 21% effective January 1, 2018, broadened the base to which U.S. income tax applies, imposed a one-time deemedrepatriation tax on ne
t unremitted earnings of foreign subsidiaries not previously subject to U.S. income tax and changed how foreign earnings are subject to U.S.income tax.
In response to the Tax Act, the Secu
rities and Exchange Commission staff issued Staff Accounting Bulletin No. 118 (“SAB 118”) which provided guidance onaccounting for the impa
ct of the Tax Act. SAB 118 allowed companies to record provisional amounts to the extent they were reasonably estimable and adjust themover time as more info
rmation became available, not to extend beyond the measurement period of one year from the enactment of the Tax Act.As a result of the Tax Act, our blend
ed U.S. statutory federal income tax rate was 33.7%  for fiscal 2018. In addition, we recorded provisional tax expense in fiscal2018 of 
$283 million . The  $283 million included a  $209 million  charge associated with th e deemed repatriation tax and a $74 million  charge related to the revaluation of deferred tax a

title: Other Legal Proceedings
heading: Other Legal Proceedings
start_phrase: We are involved in various o ther legal proceedings arising in the normal course of conducting business.
summary:
- Overview of securities class action IBEW Local 98 Pension Fund v. Best Buy Co., Inc., et al.:
  - Initially certified as a class (Aug 6, 2014) for purchasers of Best Buy common stock between Sept 14, 2010 (10:00 a.m. EDT) and Dec 13, 2010.
  - 8th Circuit granted interlocutory appeal and reversed class certification (Apr 12, 2016); rehearing en banc denied (June 1, 2016).
  - Trial court denied plaintiffs’ renewed bid for class certification (June 23, 2017) and leave to file a second amended complaint (Magistrate denial July 11, 2018; affirmed Aug 24, 2018).
  - Summary judgment granted to Best Buy dismissing remaining claims with prejudice (Mar 8, 2019).
  - Company states allegations lack merit and it intends to vigorously defend.

- Shareholder derivative actions:
  - Talluto v. Schulze, et al. and Himmel v. Best Buy consolidated into In Re: Best Buy Co., Inc. Shareholder Derivative Litigation; stayed pending discovery in IBEW.
  - Allegations include breaches of fiduciary duty, violations of Exchange Act Section 10(b)/Rule 10b-5, failure to correct misstatements about fiscal 2011 earnings projections, and insider trading by certain directors.
  - Khuong Tran derivative action filed June 2015; also stayed; voluntarily dismissed without prejudice (Mar 21, 2019).
  - Plaintiffs seek damages, interest, equitable relief, and costs; company believes claims lack merit and cannot estimate a range of possible losses.

- Other legal proceedings:
  - Routine matters in the normal course of business.
  - Probable and estimable liabilities accrued but not material to consolidated financial position, results of operations, or cash flows.
  - Additional losses, if any, cannot be reasonably estimated; resolutions not expected to be material.

- Commitments:
  - Outstanding letters of credit totaling $92 million as of Feb 2, 2019.

- Segment and geographic information:
  - Chief Operating Decision Maker is the CEO.
  - Two reportable segments:
    - Domestic: all U.S. states, districts, and territories, including GreatCall.
    - International: operations in Canada and Mexico.
  - CODM allocates resources and monitors performance at the enterprise, Domestic, and International levels; segment management handles operating decisions and performance within their segments.

summary: This partial document comes from Best Buy Co., Inc.’s SEC annual report filing and contains the Signatures section required under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. It records the company’s execution of the report on March 28, 2019, signed by Chairman and CEO Hubert Joly (principal executive officer), CFO Corie Barry (principal financial officer), SVP, Controller and Chief Accounting Officer Mathew R. Watson (principal accounting officer), and multiple directors, including Lisa M. Caputo, J. Patrick Doyle, Russell P. Fradin, Kathy J. Higgins Victor, David W. Kenny, Karen A. McLoughlin, Thomas L. Millner, Claudia F. Munce, Richelle P. Parham, Cindy R. Kent, and Eugene A. Woods. It also includes Schedule II: Valuation and Qualifying Accounts, presenting a three-year rollforward of the allowance for doubtful accounts for fiscal years ended February 2, 2019; February 3, 2018; and January 28, 2017. The schedule shows beginning balances, charges to expenses or other accounts, “other” activity (comprising bad debt write-offs, recoveries, and foreign currency effects), and ending balances, with ending allowance balances of $23 million (2019), $37 million (2018), and $52 million (2017).
